591	### 5.10 Artifacts (D22–D27)
592	
593	Owner session 2026-10-13, grilled over two rounds; the task is tsk-4, with tsk-3 (preview comments and the canvas
594	panel) under it. This section supersedes §5.7 "Canvas" and the surfaces of D18–D20; D19's store and D20's comment
595	semantics continue inside it. DESIGN.md "Artifact panel, canvas and ink" decides every pixel; WORDS.md carries the
596	terms.
597	
598	**One concept.** An **artifact** is a document a session made that you work in, kept by the hub per session. Three
599	kinds: a **page** (HTML the agent wrote: a decision page, a form, a mockup), a **canvas** (an Excalidraw drawing by
600	you or the agent) and a **preview** (a dev server or folder shown live through the existing proxy). One store, one
601	overlay, one bridge and one panel serve all three; a project's artifacts are the same panel at project scope. The
602	§5.7 pannable surface on Svelte Flow is dropped.
603	
604	**The document (D23).** One Yjs doc per artifact, which the hub syncs (the y-websocket protocol over the preview
605	listener) and persists as its update log in hub SQLite; every view of the artifact (the panel, the iOS web view, a
606	tab of its own) opens the same doc and converges. Its maps:
607	- `state`: every page field by its `name` or `id` (input, select, textarea, contenteditable) plus picks, notes and
608	  dials; `data-cawco-choice` stays for custom widgets. Keys outlive revisions, as picks do today.
609	- `elements`: the canvas, bound with `y-excalidraw` (element-level last-writer-wins by `version` and `versionNonce`,
610	  Excalidraw's own `reconcileElements` rule; an element being edited locally is never overwritten).
611	- `ink`: stroke groups, each stored relative to the box of the deepest element containing it, with its page
612	  coordinates and the anchor's selector and source.
613	- `comments` and `pins`: tsk-3's design (numbered pins, comment cards with replies, resolve and reopen).
614	The agent reads a JSON snapshot (state, pins, comments, and for a canvas the **outline**) and writes JSON patches,
615	applied as one Y transaction. A write that lands on an element you changed since the agent last read is applied and
616	flagged in the tool's result. The doc survives closing the panel, a refresh and a device change.
617	
618	**Live updates.** The agent re-publishes a page and the overlay morphs the live DOM with idiomorph (`restoreFocus`,
619	the active field's value kept): focus, scroll, typed values and bound fields survive, as hot module reload keeps
620	state. A canvas changes in place through the Y binding; it never reloads. A morph or a remote element change waits
621	for pointer-up and field blur, so nothing moves under a hand. A dev-server preview keeps its own HMR.
622	
623	**Delivery to the agent.** Changes batch into one message after 3 s of quiet (`--dur-wait-grace` × 3), and go at
624	once while the session's turn is running, so an agent mid-conversation sees you answering as it goes. Send ("Send N")
625	still says "that's all": it carries unsent pins, comments and picks as one turn, as tsk-3 decided.
626	
627	**Its own tab.** "Open in a new tab" opens the dashboard's artifact route with the panel's full chrome and the same
628	doc, never the raw proxied page. The overlay's transport is one seam: the parent window (iframe), the WebKit handler
629	(iOS), or a direct hub socket (a tab of its own).
630	
631	**The panel.** Every session has an artifact panel: the preview sheet's recipe (beside the transcript on wide screens
632	and iPad, the drawer on phones), listing the session's artifacts newest first, its head carrying the open artifact's
633	name as the title control (the Claude-panel reference) with Open in new tab, Dock/Undock, Share, and Close. Inside a
634	project, the agent can escalate an artifact into the repository at `artifacts/<name>/` (the doc's files and a
635	snapshot), git-versioned like decisions.
636	
637	**The canvas (D24, D25).** `@excalidraw/excalidraw` in the overlay's host page with its own chrome hidden and our
638	tool rail over it on house tokens. iPad: Excalidraw's pen mode (finger pans, pencil draws, pressure recorded);
639	elsewhere a tool is picked and drawn with. **Shape recognition is ours and in v1:** hold the pencil still at the end
640	of a stroke for `--dur-press-hold` and the stroke snaps to a line, arrow, rectangle, ellipse or triangle (the shape
641	element replaces the freedraw element), as Notes and Freeform do. The agent reads an **outline** (one line per
642	element: id, type, text, box, arrow bindings; ink collapsed to a count and what it sits over) plus a PNG; it writes
643	skeleton elements (`convertToExcalidrawElements`) or Mermaid (`@excalidraw/mermaid-to-excalidraw`); the
644	`.excalidraw` file is the truth. A send carries the file, the outline and the PNG through the existing
645	`attachments`/`images` contract. The pen swipe makes a **draft** canvas; the first send makes it an artifact the
646	agent holds; the agent creates and edits canvases on its own.
647	
648	**Entrances and motion (D26).** A pen swipe up on the composer (the iPad app, and the web on any pen device) opens a
649	canvas; touch type decides, so a finger's swipe stays the recall wheel and the pencil is removed from the wheel's
650	recognizer. Also Attach → Draw, ⌘⇧D on the web, and the panel's +. The pill keeps its three boxes. The pill grows
651	out of its top edge as it does for the wheel and keeps going until the canvas stands above the field, **the field
652	staying below to type**; its top edge drags to resize (floor 40 % of the column). **Dock** sends it to the side as
653	the preview tool stands, a shared-element flight; the field gives its room back on the composer's clock. Done folds
654	it back into a chip; Send flies the chip into the transcript row. A phone has no swipe: Attach → Draw, the morph to
655	the window's height, Dock to the drawer.
656	
657	**Ink on any artifact (D27).** Ink lives in the overlay for every platform: an SVG layer in the page's document,
658	strokes rendered with `perfect-freehand` from Pointer Events (`pointerType: "pen"`, `pressure`, tilt; coalesced and
659	predicted events for smoothing). Pencil draws at once, a finger scrolls and taps, the pencil's double-tap toggles the
660	eraser; Comment mode (tsk-3's Select → Comment, key C) stays for taps. After a stroke, an icon stands at its end;
661	press-and-drag opens a radial menu of four: **Annotate** (a numbered pin on the elements under the ink, no note),
662	**Comment** (a pin with a thread, stored at once), **Illustrate** (ink kept as a drawing, bound to nothing, sent as a
663	picture), **Erase**. Ignored ink is an illustration on the next Send. Ink is re-anchored by selector after a
664	revision; unplaceable ink goes to the comments' "moved" tray. The selection chip, its popover and `selection.md` are
665	deleted (tsk-3).
666	
667	**Tools** (written with `writing-for-agents`; each has a `cawco` CLI equivalent under the same role checks;
668	`show_preview` and `read_choices` are replaced, not aliased):
669	
670	| Tool | Does | Takes | Answers |
671	|---|---|---|---|
672	| `artifact_create` | Makes an artifact and shows it in the session's panel. A `page` takes HTML; a `canvas` takes skeleton elements or Mermaid; a `preview` takes a dir or port on a machine. | `kind`, `name`, one of `html` / `elements` / `mermaid` / `dir` / `port` | the artifact's id, its route, and for a canvas its outline with the ids assigned |
673	| `artifact_update` | Changes an artifact in place. A page takes new HTML (morphed) or a JSON patch of `state`; a canvas takes elements to add or replace by id, ids to delete, or Mermaid to append. | `id`, one of `html` / `patch` / `elements` / `delete` / `mermaid` | the outline after the change; each element the person changed since the last read, flagged |
674	| `artifact_read` | Reads an artifact's current state: fields, picks, pins and comments, and for a canvas the outline; `png: true` adds a picture. Works after the panel is closed. | `id`, `png?` | the snapshot; a `since` cursor for the next read |
675	| `artifact_show` | Brings an artifact to the front of the panel (the person's newest view). | `id` | opened, or why not (the session has no viewer) |
676	| `artifact_promote` | Writes an artifact into the project's repository at `artifacts/<name>/` and commits it. Refused outside a project. | `id` | the commit, the path |
677	| `comment_read` / `comment_reply` / `comment_resolve` | tsk-3, unchanged. | | |
678	
679	Completion: a tool answers only what the hub stored; nothing is reported as shown until the panel acknowledged it.
680	
681	Promote is the agent's (the person asks for it in chat); the panel's menu tags a promoted artifact "Promoted <short
682	commit>". A person's own Promote control in the panel is a one-line proposal left for later, not built.
683	
684	**Proof (no unit tests).** One seam: the hub's artifact API (REST, the sync endpoint, the tools over it), driven by
685	probe-kit specs through the real dashboard with a real page under the overlay, asserting on the hub's read of the doc
686	and on engine geometry; the MCP tools through the MCP bridge script. iOS: the simulator probe reading the composer's
687	DEBUG swipe log, extended to the pen swipe and the morph's frames; the web view's content is the same overlay. The
688	live check is the owner's: a canvas drawn with the pencil on the iPad reaches the agent as an outline and a picture,
689	the agent's edit shows on the iPad without a reload, and a re-published form keeps what was typed.
690	
691	**Not in scope.** Mac Catalyst; awareness cursors (single operator); a drawing engine of our own; tldraw.
692	
693	## 6. New primitives (gaps found)
694	
695	| Primitive | Why | Phase |

Bun's bundler implements a `--compile` flag for generating a standalone binary from a TypeScript or JavaScript file.

Bun bundles all imported files and packages into the executable, along with a copy of the Bun runtime. All built-in Bun and Node.js APIs are supported.

Set the `BUN_BE_BUN=1` environment variable to run a standalone executable as if it were the `bun` CLI itself. The executable ignores its bundled entrypoint and exposes the full `bun` CLI instead.

## API reference#

The `compile` option in `Bun.build()` accepts three forms:

```
interface BuildConfig {
  entrypoints: string[];
  compile: boolean | Bun.Build.CompileTarget | CompileBuildOptions;
  // ... other BuildConfig options (minify, sourcemap, define, plugins, etc.)
}

interface CompileBuildOptions {
  target?: Bun.Build.CompileTarget; // Cross-compilation target
  outfile?: string; // Output executable path
  assets?: string[]; // Files/directories to embed under import.meta.dir
  execArgv?: string[]; // Runtime arguments (process.execArgv)
  executablePath?: string; // Bun executable to use instead of downloading one for target
  autoloadTsconfig?: boolean; // Load tsconfig.json (default: false)
  autoloadPackageJson?: boolean; // Load package.json (default: false)
  autoloadDotenv?: boolean; // Load .env files (default: true)
  autoloadBunfig?: boolean; // Load bunfig.toml (default: true)
  bytecodeOrder?: string | string[] | false | null; // Order file(s) to lay the bytecode out by (requires bytecode: true)
  jitPolicy?: number; // JIT tier-up threshold scale at startup (default: 1 = normal)
  windows?: {
    icon?: string; // Path to .ico file
    hideConsole?: boolean; // Hide console window
    title?: string; // Application title
    publisher?: string; // Publisher name
    version?: string; // Version string
    description?: string; // Description

  };
}

Title: Bun.build function | API Reference | Bun
URL: https://bun.com/reference/bun/build
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
- compile?: boolean | CompileTarget | CompileBuildOptions

Create a standalone executable or self-contained HTML.

When `true`, creates an executable for the current platform. When a target string, creates an executable for that platform.

When used with `target: "browser"`, produces self-contained HTML files with all scripts, styles, and assets inlined. All ` ` tags become inline ` ` with bundled code, all ` ` tags become inline ` ` tags, and all asset references become `data:` URIs. All entrypoints must be HTML files. Cannot be used with `splitting`.

```
// Create executable for current platform
await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ['./app.js'],
  compile: {
    target: 'linux-x64',
  },
  outfile: './my-app'
});

// Cross-compile for Linux x64
await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ['./app.js'],
  compile: 'linux-x64',
  outfile: './my-app'
});

// Produce self-contained HTML
await Bun.build({
  entrypoints: ['./index.html'],
  target: 'browser',
  compile: true,
});
```

Title: Use Bun's package manager from a built single-executable app · Issue #16262 · oven-sh/bun
URL: https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/issues/16262
Published: 2025-01-08T00:00:00.000Z
Author: CosmoMyzrailGorynych
Highlights:
> Bun won't have a package management API in the near future, but bun could be modified to allow getting access to the main cli from a compiled binary
> 
> ```diff
> diff --git a/src/StandaloneModuleGraph.zig b/src/StandaloneModuleGraph.zig
> index aae3c32a1..14b4b9fdd 100644
> --- a/src/StandaloneModuleGraph.zig
> +++ b/src/StandaloneModuleGraph.zig
> @@ -786,6 +786,12 @@ pub const StandaloneModuleGraph = struct {
> const self_exe = openSelf() catch return null;
> defer _ = Syscall.close(self_exe);
> 
> + if (bun.getenvZ("BUN_SKIP_STANDALONE_MODULE_GRAPH")) |v| {
> + if (v.len > 0 and !(v.len == 1 and v[0] == '0')) {
> + return null;
> + }
> + }
> +
> var trailer_bytes: [4096]u8 = undefined;
> std.posix.lseek_END(self_exe.cast(), -4096) catch return null;
> ```
> 
> With this change, running a compiled binary with `BUN_SKIP_STANDALONE_MODULE_GRAPH=1` gives access to the regular bun commands
...
> `BUN_BE_BUN` flag env var option has been added so you can manually force it like @pfgithub's above solution (#20251). I'm not sure how well it actually works for `bun install` though as I know it sometimes launches sub-processes.
> 
> To try it out, you can `bun upgrade --canary`
...
> Thanks for the request. The env-flag approach discussed here shipped as `BUN_BE_BUN=1` (#20251): running a compiled executable with that variable set gives you the regular bun CLI, and install, add, remove, update and pm ls all work from a compiled binary, so we're closing this out. A JS-level package-manager API is still a separate request.
> 
> **What I ran** (in Docker, `oven/bun:1.3.14` vs canary `1.4.0-canary.1`):
> 
> ```sh
> echo 'console.log("APP_MAIN_RAN")' > app.js
> bun build --compile ./app.js --outfile ./myapp
> ./myapp install # prints APP_MAIN_RAN
> mkdir proj && cd proj && echo '{"name":"proj","dependencies":{"is-number":"7.0.0"}}' > package.json
> BUN_BE_BUN=1 ../myapp install
> BUN_BE_BUN=1 ../myapp add left-pad@1.3.0
> BUN_BE_BUN=1 ../myapp pm ls
> BUN_BE_BUN=1 ../myapp remove left-pad
> BUN_BE_BUN=1 ../myapp update
> ```
> 
> **Results**
> 
> - **Bun 1.3.14:** compiled exe ran its own entrypoint normally, and with BUN_BE_BUN=1 acted as the bun CLI — install/add/pm ls/remove/update all exit 0, is-number installed and left-pad added then removed; printed OK line. Feature already present.
> - **Canary:** same — plain run printed APP_MAIN_RAN, BUN_BE_BUN=1 gave `bun install v1.4.0-canary.1`, add/pm ls/remove/update all exit 0, printed OK line.
> 
> It works on both Bun 1.3.14 and the current canary, so you shouldn't need to upgrade for it — if it still misbehaves for you, comment here and we'll reopen.

text: The user answered: "Live Svelte components, on any installed CawCo with nothing extra on the user's machine: which engine compiles the component the agent writes?"="how are you going to do it". Read the answers carefully — they may request clarification, changes, or that you not proceed — and follow what they actually say.

Here's how I'd build it, concretely.

**What the agent does**
1. It writes a normal `.svelte` file in its checkout, for example `previews/TranscriptCards.svelte`. The file imports the project's real components (`$lib/cawco/transcript/ToolCard.svelte` and so on), passes them mock props, and lays out the variants side by side.
2. It calls `artifact_create(kind: "preview", svelte: "previews/TranscriptCards.svelte")` once. After that, every save re-renders the panel. There's no tool call per change, the same way Pencil and Paper behave.

**What cawco does on that machine (all in-process, inside the binary)**
1. It watches the file. On each save it runs `Bun.build` on a small generated entry that imports the file and calls Svelte's `mount`.
2. A plugin that compiles `.svelte` and `.svelte.ts` files uses the `svelte/compiler` bundled inside cawco. `Bun.build` runs inside a compiled Bun binary; I tested it on our Bun 1.4.2.
3. Imports resolve the way the project's own build resolves them:
   - aliases from `svelte.config.js` and `tsconfig` paths (`$lib`);
   - relative files from disk;
   - third-party packages from the project's `node_modules`.
4. `svelte` itself always resolves to cawco's own copy, so the whole tree uses one compiler and one runtime.
5. Component CSS is collected, plus the project's global stylesheet (its tokens and fonts), and fonts and images are carried along as assets.
6. The result (one JS module, one CSS file, the assets) is stored as a new revision of the artifact on the hub.

**What the panel does**
1. It loads the revision inside the existing artifact overlay, mounts it, and on the next revision unmounts and remounts with the same props.
2. Picks, comments and ink work exactly as they do on pages today.
3. The iPhone and iPad apps only display the result, so they need nothing new.
4. A compile error shows in the panel with its file and line, and the agent gets it as well.

**Not proven yet, so the spike goes first, on your real case (the transcript cards that cost 3.5 hours)**
- Whether the cockpit dashboard's real `transcript/*.svelte` components compile and render this way, `$lib` imports and all.
- Tailwind v4: its compiler is a native addon. I need to prove it can live inside the binary, or whether a project using Tailwind needs another path.
- How long a save takes before the panel updates. I'll measure it; I'm not quoting a number I haven't seen.

If you're happy with this plan, I'll brief that spike to a leaf. It comes back with those three answers and a live panel rendering the real transcript cards from a `.svelte` file.

Fixing it took three product fixes: pins written in the iOS app were never delivered to the session, a page tap that closed an open pin card never reached the page, and the card could close while a finger was still down on the page.

The simulator slot was deleted by mac-slot when the run ended.

Run 2 (before the fixes) had 4 FAILs, each traced to its line:
1. "a tap on the page outside the card closes it, the page still takes the tap": "dismissed by=page … the page did not take it". Closing the card sends the overlay `cawco:track-pin null`, and `pins.ts` `track` ran `draw()`, which removes and re-appends every disc. iOS WebKit's content-change observer saw new content during the tap and suppressed the click (no `preview answered` navigation line followed). Fix: `track` redraws only when a resolved pin's disc must appear or go (`onIt`); otherwise it calls `tell()`.
2. "Send 1 …": stale probe step. Send for pins was removed in 1a59485f5 (automatic delivery). Run 3 then exposed a real bug: no delivery note ever came, and the reply was stamped `sentAt` 20 ms after it was written. The iOS app reads pins via comment_read's HTTP route on the writer's session (Comments.swift:87), and since 283cfdc4f every read there stamped pins heard (`service.ts` `readHeard`). Every pin the app showed was therefore marked heard and never delivered. Fix: the comment_read tool sends `reader=session` (delegation-tools.ts), the route passes it (routes.ts), and commentRead stamps heard only for that read (service.ts). 283cfdc4f's protection, that what the session itself reads counts as heard, is kept. openapi.json was regenerated (the openapi:check required it). Other callers of the route: the iOS app, this probe, and probe-kit artifacts.ts:683, which only waits for the pin and doesn't rely on stamping.
3. Long thread, and 4. Resolve: knock-on effects of 2. With Send gone the keyboard stayed up over a 134 pt well, so the card scrolled by design (Pins.swift fitRoom) and put Resolve at y −350. The probe now closes the card with its Close after the delivery check.

Also changed in PreviewController.swift: a `cawco:press` from the page now closes the card when the finger lifts. The window PressWatcher hears the page's touches for their lift only, and a touch taken by a scroll also closes, as pointerdown does on the web. This matches the outside-press rule documented at :1070 and covers a card closing with the keyboard up. Probe determinism (uninstall before install) landed earlier in 1d9389f59.

Title: Code on Canvas
URL: https://docs.pen.dev/core-concepts/code-on-canvas
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
pen.dev uses the Script node to bring code to the canvas. Drop one onto the canvas, point it at a `.js` file, and the script’s output renders as nested layers — pie charts, grids, decorative patterns, anything you can describe in code.
...
1. Open the Shape tool dropdown in the toolbar.
2. Pick Script (the `</>` icon).
3. Click anywhere on the canvas to drop a 200×200 script node.
...
In the properties panel, type a path into the script field. Paths are resolved relative to your `.pen` file, so a sibling file is just `chart.js`. Save the JS file in the same folder as the `.pen` file (or any subfolder) and reference it from there.
...
1. Grab a ready-made script. Browse highagency/pencil-scripts for example scripts maintained by the pen.dev team (charts, grids, patterns, and more) and drop them next to your `.pen` file as a starting point.
2. Ask the AI agent. Open the agent panel and describe what you want — it will create the `.js` file for you and link it to the selected script node.
...
As soon as the file resolves, the script runs and its output appears inside the node’s bounds.
...
- Resize the node — drag the handles to resize the node, or change the size in the properties panel. The script re-runs and the layout reflows live.
- Use the input controls — every `@input` line in the script header becomes a control in the properties panel. Numbers, strings, booleans, colors, enum dropdowns, and references to existing components are all supported. Editing a control re-runs the script instantly.
- Edit the `.js` file — the desktop app and IDE extension watch the file on disk. Save in your editor and the canvas updates without a reload.
- Convert to layers — whenever you need to edit the generated content by hand, click the button at the bottom of the properties panel. The script node is replaced with a regular frame containing a snapshot of the generated layers.
...
- The `.js` file lives outside the `.pen` file. The script node only stores a path to it. Multiple script nodes can point at the same file; each gets its own size and input values.
- Inputs are declared in the file header. The `@input` lines in the header comment tell pen.dev which controls to render in the properties panel. Rename or remove an input in the file and the panel updates.
- Scripts return an array of nodes. Each returned object uses the same schema as the rest of pen.dev and is inserted as a child of the script node.
- Output is derived state. Generated children re-render every time the script runs and are not part of the undo history. To turn them into editable layers, use Convert to layers.
...
Every script starts with a header comment declaring its schema version and the inputs it exposes.
...
- `@schema` — required. Use the version declared by `Document.version` in the TypeScript schema.
- `@input` — zero or more. Each one becomes a control in the properties panel. The name is also the key used on `pencil.input`.
...
| Type | Example | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `number` | `@input size: number(min=0, max=100) = 10` | Optional `min` / `max` named args clamp the value before the script runs. |
| `string` | `@input label: string = "Hello"` | Multi-line text in the panel. |
| `boolean` | `@input filled: boolean = true` | Rendered as a checkbox. |
| `color` | `@input fill: color = #3B82F6` | Hex literal or a quoted string. |
| `enum` | `@input layout: enum("grid", "stack") = "grid"` | Positional list of quoted options, rendered as a dropdown. |
| `ref` | `@input target: ref` | Reference to a reusable component, picked from a thumbnail grid. |
...
Your script body runs with a single `pencil` argument:

| Field | Type | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `pencil.width` | `number` | Current width of the script node. |
| `pencil.height` | `number` | Current height of the script node. |
| `pencil.input. ` | matches the `@input` type | Current value of the named input. Numbers are clamped to their declared limits; enums must match a declared option. |
...
- The script must `return` an array of node objects. Each object follows the .pen format.
- Script output can contain at most 1000 nodes, including nested children, and cannot define reusable components. The script must finish within 2 seconds.
...
const rows = Math.floor(pencil.input.rows);
const gap = pencil.input.gap;
const rowH = (pencil.height - gap * (rows - 1)) / rows;
...
for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) {
 nodes.push({
 type: "rectangle",
 x: 0,
 y: r * (rowH + gap),
 width: pencil.width,
 height: rowH,
 cornerRadius: pencil.input.rounded ? 8 : 0,
 fill: pencil.input.fill,
 });
}

Title: The .pen Format
URL: https://docs.pencil.dev/for-developers/the-pen-format
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
pen.dev documents are stored in .pen files. This documentation is for developers who would like to read or write .pen files. Use pen.dev, its MCP tools, or the CLI to make changes instead of editing serialized IDs and references by hand.
...
- .pen files contain a JSON structure, that describes an object tree, not unlike HTML or SVG.
- Each object in the document is a graphical entity on pen.dev’s infinite two-dimensional canvas.
- The objects must have an `id` property that uniquely identifies them within the document, and a `type` field from one of the possible object types (like `rectangle`, `frame`, `text`, `script`, etc. – consult the TypeScript schema for the exhaustive list of supported types).
...
- The top-level objects in a document are placed on an infinite two-dimensional canvas. Use `x` and `y` to position their top-left corner.
- Objects nested under other objects are positioned relative to their parents’ top-left corner.
- A parent object can take over the sizing and positioning of its children using a flexbox-style layout system via properties like `layout`, `justifyContent` and `alignItems`.
- Child objects can choose to fill their parent, or use a fixed `width` and/or `height`.
- Parent objects can choose to fit the size of their children, or use a fixed `width` and/or `height`.
...
A key difference between pen.dev documents and HTML or SVG is that pen.dev documents allow reusing existing chunks of the object tree at different places. This enables the building of reusable components, that can be used as concise building blocks for more complicated structures.
...
When an object is marked with the property `reusable: true`, it becomes a reusable component:
...
The object type `ref` is used to create an instance of such components:
...
An instance replicates everything under the component root:
...
Here `red-round-button` will have an identical `"Submit"` label as `round-button`. But this label, too, can be customized using the `descendants` property:
...
Components can be built from instances of other components:
...
their IDs with the containing instance’s ID and a slash in the `desc
...
In addition to customization, an object inside an instance can be completely replaced with new object:
...
Alternatively to 1:1 replacement, an object can be kept as is, and we can replace only its `children` with new objects:
...
This children replacement mechanism is ideal for container-style components, like panels, cards, windows, sidebars, etc.
...
When a frame inside a component is intended to have its children replaced (e.g. the content holder frame inside a panel), it can be marked with the `slot` property:
...
pen.dev displays such slots with a special effect, and lets users insert instances of the suggested components (i.e. `round-button` or `icon-button` above) with a single click.
...
/** Container to create hierarchy and layout. default layout=horizontal, width=fit_content, height=fit_content, clip=false. */
export interface Frame extends Rectangleish, CanHaveChildren, Layout {
 type: "frame";
 /** Clip overflow. Default false. */
 clip?: BooleanOrVariable;
 placeholder?: boolean;
 /** Marks frame as a slot for component instances. Array entries are IDs of recommended reusable child components (e.g. menu items inside a menu bar). */
 slot?: false | string[];
}
...
export interface Script

## How it works

 

1. When you create an app, we load the code into a web container
2. The container runs and serves the code
3. Our editor receives the preview link and displays it in an iFrame
4. Our editor reads and indexes the code from the container
5. We instrument the code in order to map elements to their place in code
6. When the element is edited, we edit the element in our iFrame, then in code
7. Our AI chat also has code access and tools to understand and edit the code

This architecture can theoretically scale to any language or framework that
displays DOM elements declaratively (e.g. jsx/tsx/html). We are focused on
making it work well with Next.js and TailwindCSS for now.

Onlook is technically a browser that points to your localhost running the app. It can manipulate the DOM like a Chrome Devtool, and all these changes are injected into the page through a CSS stylesheet or DOM manipulation. The changes are non-persistent until written to code.

To translate the changes to code, we inject an attribute into the DOM elements at build-time that points back to the code like a sourcemap. The attribute gives us the location of the code block, and the component scope [1]. We then find the code, parse it into an AST, inject the styles, then write it back.
...
This technique is framework agnostic as we can swap in a different compiler for another framework[2]. It can work for any codebase as we’re just using open standards that don’t require any custom code. The code generated is written directly into your codebase, locally, so you can always take the output without being locked-in to the tool.

AI agents are getting more powerful every day; they can not only read, but also see and think. Collaborating with agents is more than just code generation these days. You can now bring agents to a canvas and we built Paper for that.

The visual tool shouldn’t replace the code. The problem is that the canvas never learned to speak the same language. There wasn’t a tool based on HTML and CSS that made it easy for agents to work with. And that’s why Paper exists.

We needed to rethink the foundations and finally build something that exports code, imports React components, fetches APIs and lets you iterate quickly—but 20 years of digital design should compound with that, not reset. We need a new standard. A more connected environment where you can go from design to code and back whenever you want without much of the drama.

...
The canvas needs to be made of the same material as the product. Imagine a surface where “designing” isn’t just drawing a picture of your component, but actual React code that can be exported. A place where HTML and CSS are the medium, and the output.

This is the part that changes the whole dynamic: it goes both ways. You can pull reality onto the canvas when you need to go wide, and you can push decisions back into code when you need to go narrow—without turning either side into a dead end.

Sloppy outputs aren’t about agents failing—they’re about understanding and instructions not being there. You can now give your agents a whole website to build, with all the annotations you want. Plan mode just got better. It’s a living spec for building with agents.

Infinite power without a map is chaos. The canvas gives us that map—to ... the dots and ... agents do their thing. Your other question: no, I hadn't looked at how Pencil and Paper actually do it before my last two answers. I have now:

**pen.dev (Pencil)** never renders your code components (docs.pen.dev).
- Its canvas is its own `.pen` format: "a JSON structure, that describes an object tree, not unlike HTML or SVG".
- It has its own reusable components (`reusable: true`), instances by `ref`, and `slot`s you drop components into.
- Code to design means the agent recreates your component in that format: "Ask the agent to read an existing component and recreate it on the canvas."
- The live parts are a Script node, a `.js` file it watches and re-renders on save, and a Browser node, a "live web page shown on canvas".

**Paper** builds its canvas from real HTML and CSS (paper.design/docs/mcp: "Paper is built on HTML and CSS, which LLMs already understand well").
- Agents write HTML into it over MCP and pull tokens from your CSS variables.
- It exports React or Tailwind.
- Using your code components is on its roadmap, not shipped ("Use your code components… one source of truth"), and it's React.

**What renders your real components and lets you assemble and edit them:**
- **Onlook** (open source) does exactly that, for React only. It runs your app in a container and reads your Storybook stories for the components. It tags each element in the DOM with the source location it came from, so an edit on the canvas becomes a precise code edit (AST patch).
- **Designbook** (React) injects into your app's Vite dev server, so it also needs Vite.
- **Layrr** (AGPL) reverse-proxies your dev server and claims Svelte. It also needs a running dev server.
- **For Svelte, workshops that render real components:** Storybook with Svelte CSF (Svelte 5 supported), and poveste, a maintained successor to Histoire with Svelte 5 support. In Svelte CSF, a `<Story asChild>` composes real components, which is exactly "assemble them". Every one of these needs the project's Vite.

**What that means for us:**
- Nobody ships this for Svelte inside a compiled app. Every tool above runs on the project's own dev server, and that's what your installed-binary requirement rules out.
- **Reuse:** the file format for assembling components should be Storybook's Svelte CSF stories, an existing standard, rather than one we invent.
- **Editing:** take Onlook's mechanism, the DOM element mapped to its source location and edited precisely. Whether Svelte's dev compile already carries those locations I still have to verify; my check failed because the shared tree has no `node_modules`.
- **Ours to build:** only the compile step inside cawco, which I've shown runs inside a compiled Bun binary.

THE QUESTION. What is the best technical design for CawCo's "live components": an agent creates, reuses, assembles and edits a project's real UI components, rendered live in CawCo's artifact panel, the way pen.dev and Paper work with agents? It has to work for every CawCo user, whatever language or framework their project uses.

WHAT CAWCO IS AND HAS:
- A fleet control plane. One compiled Bun binary per machine (hub + agent).

- Sessions work in git workspaces on the user's machines.

- One Yjs doc per artifact (fields, picks, pins, comments, ink), pins anchored to elements and carrying file:line, and a per-project mockup library in OpenUI Lang over the project's own design system (tokens, fonts, assets).

EVIDENCE GATHERED (each with its source):
- pen.dev (docs.pen.dev): its canvas is its own `.pen` JSON ("a JSON structure, that describes an object tree, not unlike HTML or SVG").
  - It has reusable components (`reusable: true`, `ref` instances, `slot`s).
  - Code to design is the agent recreating the component: "Ask the agent to read an existing component and recreate it on the canvas."
  - Live parts: a Script node (a watched `.js` file whose output renders as layers) and a Browser node ("Live web page shown on canvas").
  - Agents connect via MCP (`execute`, `get_app_state`).
- Paper (paper.design/docs/mcp; blog "A real space to design in the age of agents"): the canvas is real HTML/CSS ("Paper is built on HTML and CSS, which LLMs already understand well").
  - Agents write HTML into it via MCP and sync tokens from CSS variables. It exports React/Tailwind.
  - Its roadmap lists "Use your code components … one source of truth", so that isn't shipped yet, and it's React.
- Onlook (github.com/onlook-dev/onlook, MIT-family, React/Next only): "we load the code into a web container … displays it in an iFrame … instrument the code in order to map elements to their place in code … edit the element in our iFrame, then in code".
  - It reads the project's Storybook stories as the components on its canvas.
  - Desktop wiki: it injects a source-pointing attribute at build time, then parses the file and patches it as an AST.
- Designbook (React): injects into the app's own Vite dev server. Layrr (AGPL): reverse-proxies the user's dev server, claims React/Vue/Svelte.
- code-inspector-plugin (github.com/zh-lx/code-inspector): bundlers "webpack / vite / rspack / rsbuild / farm / esbuild / turbopack / mako"; frameworks "vue2 / vue3 / nuxt / react / nextjs / umijs / preact / solid / qwik / svelte / astro". It injects element→source location in dev.
- Svelte 5.57.1 dev compile already sets `element.__svelte_meta = { parent, loc: { file, line, column } }` (`$.add_locations`).
- Storybook Component Story Format is a cross-framework story standard. Svelte CSF (`@storybook/addon-svelte-csf` v5) composes real components with `<Story asChild>`. poveste (Histoire successor) supports Svelte 5 and Vue. All of these run through the project's own Vite.
- Svelte's team on compiling in the browser: "rather involved and also slow, so I definitely do not recommend doing this" (sveltejs/svelte#15658). The svelte.dev playground does it anyway in a worker with rollup and CDN npm.
- `Bun.build` runs inside a `bun build --compile` binary (tested on CawCo's Bun 1.4.2). Bun has an official Svelte plugin. Bun PR #32262 adds an opt-out runtime that strips Bun.build (`--compile-runtime=full` keeps it).

  - compose with CSF stories over real components;

4. Coverage: which stacks work in v1, and what a non-web stack (SwiftUI, Flutter, React Native) gets.
5. The agent tools (artifact_create/update shape changes) and what the panel shows in each state: starting, compiling, error with file:line, live.
6. What must be proven first (the riskiest assumptions), as a short ordered list of probes with pass/fail criteria.
7. What would change your recommendation.

**Why it switched to medium**

You set this session to `xhigh`; nothing you did switched it back. Here's what happened:

1. Yesterday at 16:49 the session was continued into a fresh conversation (CawCo's `continue_session`). That relaunch carries the model and harness but no effort, so Claude Code started at its own default, which is `medium` on every one of your accounts.
2. The hub then copied the effort Claude Code reported back into this session's record, overwriting your `xhigh`.
3. Every relaunch after that (five account moves on usage limits, the last at 01:33) faithfully carried `--effort=medium`.

So from yesterday afternoon until you switched it back, this chat ran at medium. That likely explains a lot of today.

A leaf (bb2644e8) is fixing it at the rule:
- every relaunch, continuations included, keeps the effort you chose;
- what Claude Code reports it's running at is stored separately and can never overwrite your choice again;
- a check on a test fleet covers each relaunch path.

**The best technical solution for live components, for every framework**

This is my view; I've asked Fable to write the full spec and to challenge it.

1. **Render with the project's own toolchain, not one we carry.** Only a project's own compiler and config can faithfully render its React, Vue, Svelte, Solid or Astro components. Bundling compilers inside CawCo can't cover every framework, and the Svelte team itself advises against compiling in the browser. Nothing extra gets installed: the user's project already has its toolchain, or it couldn't run. CawCo's job is to run the project's own dev server itself, keep it alive, and show it in the panel, so no agent ever babysits a server. The dev servers dying between turns, which cost the 3.5 hours, was a CawCo bug we've since fixed.
2. **Assemble with stories.** An agent writes a story file that imports the real components with mock data, variants side by side. Storybook's Component Story Format is the existing cross-framework standard for this. A project that already has stories gets them for free, which is what Onlook does.
3. **Edit by clicking the rendered thing.** code-inspector-plugin maps each rendered element to its file, line and column, across Vite, webpack, rspack, esbuild and Turbopack, and across React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Preact, Qwik and Astro; Svelte also carries this itself. A click in the panel becomes a pin or an edit at that exact line in the real component.
4. **Before code exists, design in plain HTML and CSS over the project's tokens.** That's how Paper works, and we already have the per-project mockup library for it.
5. **Non-web stacks** (SwiftUI, Flutter) don't fit this model. Fable will spell out what they get.

**Running now:**
- **Fable (f59bb492):** writing the spec.
- **Research leaf (1f6aa735):** reading Onlook's internals, code-inspector's mechanism and licence, and CSF outside Storybook. Its findings go to Fable.
- **I'll bring you the spec and any choices that are yours to make.** Nothing gets built before you've seen it.

Main findings:
1. Onlook (Apache-2.0).
   - It writes `data-oid` into the user's source at file-write time (`packages/file-system/src/code-fs.ts`) and indexes oid → path/line/col.
   - It edits through Babel (parse, traverse, generate with `retainLines`) plus prettier.
   - Its code is JSX-bound. Only the architecture ports to Svelte: swap `data-oid` for `__svelte_meta` and Babel for `svelte/compiler` plus magic-string.
2. addon-svelte-csf (MIT).
   - Its transform depends on rollup's `this.parse` and `this.getModuleInfo`, so it is not a standalone module.
   - The parser files themselves only need `svelte/compiler`.
3. poveste (MIT).
   - It requires Vite 8 and has a Vue app shell.
   - Its story format passes helpers as an `Hst` prop, and `initState` exists because stories mount once per slot.
4. Other tools:
   - Every edit-to-source tool found (stylewright, Glide, designtools) needs a running Vite dev server.
   - The JSON-model builders (svaro, svelte-visual-builder) don't edit source.
5. REPL bundler (`@sveltejs/repl`, MIT per its package.json; the repo has no LICENSE file).
   - It uses a virtual-file map, an `options.aliases` plugin and `svelte.compile({dev:true})`.
   - It is a good blueprint for a `Bun.build` plugin but assumes a browser Worker and fetches from npm at runtime.
   - The alias resolver does not try `.svelte` suffixes.
6. code-inspector (MIT).
   - It stamps `data-insp-path="file:line:col:tag"` through per-language transforms (JSX, Vue, Svelte, Astro, MDX, Pug) across 7 bundlers.
   - It has an AI mode for claudeCode, opencode and codex.
   - It can't be added from outside as shipped: no CLI or zero-config mode. A wrapper config per bundler is my own untested idea, labelled as such.
7. Storybook.
   - Its supported-framework list is in the report.
   - `composeStories` renders CSF without Storybook's server, but it needs the framework package, and the Vitest addon needs Vite.
   - I found no formal CSF spec.
   - Onlook's open-source repo runs projects in a CodeSandbox container. The current desktop app runs the project's own dev command in a git worktree and frames the dev server. It is closed source for now.
8. Non-web stacks.
   - pen.dev and Paper (paper.design) are web-only.
   - Flutter has a scriptable previewer (`flutter widget-preview start`) with no edit-to-source.
   - SwiftUI and Compose previews are IDE-bound.
   - Composer is the only native edit-to-source tool found, and it is small.

[Report from delegate cockpit-f59bb492#0e1b409f — turn complete] Headline: Recommended design: a "stage" artifact kind. The agent writes a stage file in the project's own framework that imports the real components; CawCo's daemon runs the project's own Vite inside the workspace as a supervised host and shows it through the existing preview proxy; element-to-source comes from the framework's dev metadata; the person edits through pins and picks. No compiling in the binary or the browser. # Live components (D29) — the spec Sources: the PRD sections named in the brief, the evidence the brief carries. No repo file beyond the PRD was read and no web source was fetched; where a claim below rests on my own knowledge of Vite, SvelteKit or code-inspector-plugin rather than on the brief's evidence, it is marked "(own knowledge; probe N proves it)". ## 0. The answer in one paragraph The owner's requirement is "the project's real components, tokens, fonts and global CSS, on mock props, variants side by side", rendered live, Svelte for CawCo's own code, "for all our users, across their many languages and frameworks", from a compiled binary, without hand-rolling what exists. Only one thing satisfies "real components in the project's real context" for every framework: the project's own compiler, with the project's own config. So CawCo does not compile anything. It runs the project's toolchain for the agent, keeps it alive itself, and puts a thin contract on top: a **stage** (a component file the agent writes, in the project's language, that imports the real components and lays out variants on mock data), a **host** per toolchain (v1: Vite, which covers Svelte, SvelteKit, Vue, React, Solid, Preact, Lit, vanilla), and a **source reader** in the overlay that turns a click into `file:line:column` so pins, comments and the agent's edits land precisely. This is pen.dev's and Paper's loop (agent writes, canvas shows, person marks, agent edits) with the project's own code as the material instead of a canvas format — which is exactly what Paper lists as unshipped on its roadmap ("Use your code components … one source of truth") and what pen.dev avoids by having the agent "recreate" a component on its canvas. Onlook does it for React only by loading the code into a container, instrumenting it, and mapping elements back to source; this spec is that mechanism generalised, with the agent as the editor instead of an AST patcher. ## 1. Architecture ### 1.1 Who compiles and renders, on which machine **The workspace's machine compiles; every device renders.** The daemon on the machine that holds the workspace runs a **stage host**: the project's own Vite dev server, started programmatically from the workspace's own install (`node_modules/vite`, already present because the project builds there), inside the workspace's sandbox boundary, as a listener the daemon owns. The hub proxies it the way it proxies previews today; the dashboard panel, the artifact's own tab and the iOS/iPad web view all show the proxied URL under the existing overlay. Why the project's toolchain and nothing else: - The compiled output of `svelte/compiler` imports the Svelte runtime and the project's modules (`$lib/...`, sibling `.svelte` files, `app.css`, Tailwind, `$app/*` in SvelteKit, aliases from `vite.config`/`svelte.config`). Those resolve only under the project's Vite with its plugins. The PRD already records this (§5.10 D29) and the Svelte team's line on in-browser compiling. - The owner's references (svelte-dynamic-component-engine, svelte-runtime-components, svelte-edge) all compile **one self-contained component** with esbuild and load the Svelte runtime through an import map. That works for a component with no project imports and breaks at the first `import X from '$lib/...'`. The owner's words rule that out: "in the project's real context", "reuse components and assemble them". - `Bun.build` inside CawCo's binary (with Bun's Svelte plugin) has the same ceiling: it would re-implement the project's config (aliases, PostCSS/Tailwind, SvelteKit's virtual modules, env) and only for Svelte. Rejected, and it is not a fallback either. - Vue, React, Solid, Preact, Lit and plain TS projects all run the same host unchanged: Vite is the common compiler across them, and each project's framework plugin is already in its `node_modules`. **Owner's pick (the PRD leaves "where it compiles" open). Recommended: the project's own Vite, run by the daemon in the workspace (this spec).** The alternatives — Bun.build in the binary, or compiling in the browser — only serve components with no project imports, so they would be a different feature (a scratch component sandbox), not D29. I recommend not building either. ### 1.2 From a compiled binary, with nothing installed by CawCo CawCo's binary carries one embedded file, `host.mjs` (~ a few hundred KB): the launcher plus a Vite plugin, bundled at CawCo's build time by `Bun.build` into a single self-contained module whose only external import is `vite`, resolved from the project. On first use the daemon writes it to `/.cawco/stage/host.mjs` (the `.cawco/` dir is added to `.git/info/exclude`, never committed) and spawns it with the runtime the project already uses — `bun` if the Vite root's lockfile is `bun.lock`/`bun.lockb`, else `node`. If neither is on PATH, or no `vite` resolves from the Vite root, `artifact_create` refuses with that exact reason; nothing starts. No `npm install`, no global package, no change to the project's `package.json` or config. What `host.mjs` does (all inside the project's process, under the project's Vite): 1. `createServer({ root, configFile: , server: { host: "127.0.0.1", port: 0, hmr: { overlay: false } }, plugins: [cawcoStage()] })` — the project's config and plugins apply unchanged; ours is added. (own knowledge of Vite's API; probe 1 proves it under SvelteKit.) 2. The `cawcoStage()` plugin: - a **pre-middleware** serving `GET /__cawco/stage/`: an HTML shell built from the app's own shell (SvelteKit: `src/app.html` with `%sveltekit.*%` placeholders stripped; Vite SPA: the root `index.html` with its entry script removed) so `` attributes, theme scripts and font ``s match the app, plus one `
``` **Why not Storybook CSF as the format.** CSF is a JS object format whose execution needs the renderer package (`@storybook/svelte`'s `composeStories`, the Svelte CSF addon's preprocessor for `.stories.svelte`), i.e. packages CawCo cannot install. A component file in the project's language needs nothing and is what the agent already writes. Interop is free: a project that has stories can import them into a stage through its own `composeStories`; CawCo builds nothing for it. ## 3. The editing model **Select → source → edit, with the agent as the editor and the person as the reviewer.** - **Select.** The overlay (already injected into every preview) resolves the element under a tap or a stroke to source with one reader and one output shape `{file, line, column, component, variant}`: Svelte 5 → walk up from the element to the first node with `__svelte_meta`, take `loc`, and the component chain from `__svelte_meta.parent`; other frameworks → the vendored code-inspector attribute; the enclosing `data-cawco-variant` names the variant. Pins and ink (D27) carry this payload; today's pins already carry `file:line`, this adds `column`, `component` and `variant`. Hover outlines the element and shows `Component · file:line` in the pin tooltip. - **Source.** `artifact_read` returns pins and comments with that payload, plus `status`, `errors`, `variants` and `picks`. `comment_read` returns the same for a pin's thread. A comment on a card's title therefore reads "`EventCard.svelte:42:6` in variant `roomy`: make it heavier" — a precise edit, not a hunt. - **Edit by the agent.** It edits the component or the stage with its file tools; Vite HMR re-renders; the pin re-anchors by the existing rule (file:line, then selector, then text; unplaceable → "moved" tray); the agent resolves the pin with `comment_reply`/`comment_resolve` as today. Errors from the edit arrive through delivery within 3 s. - **Edit by the person, v1:** pins and comments (D20), picks on `data-cawco-choice` variants (D19), dials through the bridge. That is the pen.dev/Paper loop with code as the material. - **Owner's pick — direct manipulation.** Recommended: **v2, as proposals.** The overlay lets the person change text, a spacing or a colour on the selected element in place; the hub records it as an edit-proposal pin `{file, line, column, property, from, to}` which the agent applies to source and resolves. Not recommended: Onlook's path (CawCo parses and patches the AST itself) — it is a parser per framework, it is why Onlook is React-only, and the agent is already the thing that edits code. Pins and comments tie in without new storage: a stage artifact is one Yjs doc like any artifact (`state`, `pins`, `comments`, `ink`), the overlay transport is the same seam (iframe, WebKit handler, direct socket), and `artifact_promote` writes the doc snapshot to `artifacts//`; the stage file is already repo content, so promote copies nothing else. ## 4. Coverage **v1 (the Vite host):** any project where the stage's nearest `vite.config.*` root resolves `vite` ≥ 5: Svelte 5 and SvelteKit (proven first, on CawCo's dashboard), then Vue 3, React, Solid, Preact, Lit and vanilla — same host, each claimed only after its own probe (6). Source mapping: Svelte through `__svelte_meta`, the rest through the vendored transform. Not v1: Next.js (not Vite), Nuxt (Vite behind nuxi), Angular, Astro (`.astro` is server-only; its framework islands would work but are not claimed), Qwik. **Later hosts, same stage contract and tools, one host per toolchain:** - **Flutter:** a live host. `flutter run -d web-server -t .dart --web-port

` is a listener the supervisor owns; hot reload by sending `r` on its stdin; element→source through the widget inspector service (`--track-widget-creation` is on in debug), the overlay asking for the creation location under the pointer. Closest to live among non-web stacks. - **React Native (Expo):** a live-but-approximate host through `expo start --web` (react-native-web) for layout and copy; native fidelity through the snapshot host below. - **SwiftUI (and native RN):** a snapshot host on the Mac, since Xcode Previews cannot be served. The stage is a `*.stage.swift` of `#Preview("variant")` blocks; the host builds the stage scheme to the simulator and screenshots each preview with the fleet's existing xcui/MobileBuildMCP tools, publishing a page artifact of one image per variant with pins anchored by variant and the `#Preview` block's `file:line`. Minutes per round, not live; honest and still a loop. A non-web project in v1 gets nothing from this feature; it keeps `preview` and `show_image`. The tool says so by name rather than degrading. ## 5. Tools and panel states **Tools** (`artifact_*` gain a kind; `preview` stays for whole apps and folders, as D29 says the stage replaces it only "as the way an agent shows a component it made"): | Tool | Change | |---|---| | `artifact_create` | `kind: "stage"`, takes `name` and `file` (a repo-relative path under a Vite root). Answers `{ id, route, root, runtime, status, errors[], variants[] }`; waits for the first compile (cold budget 60 s) so `status` is `live` or `error` with locations; `variants` is filled when a viewer attached during the wait, else `[]`, and `opened` follows the existing completion rule (nothing reported shown until the panel acknowledged it). Refuses, with the reason, when no `vite.config.*` is above `file`, `vite` does not resolve, or no `node`/`bun` is on PATH. | | `artifact_update` | For a stage: `file` (point the artifact at another stage file) or `patch` of `state` as today. Content changes need no call: edit the file. | | `artifact_read` | Adds `status`, `errors`, `variants`; pins and comments carry `{file, line, column, component, variant}`; `outline` (rendered tree per variant with component names and boxes, read through the overlay) when a viewer is attached, else `null` with the reason. Pictures: the agent's existing browser tools on the artifact's route, which the hub proxy makes reachable. | | `artifact_show`, `artifact_promote`, `comment_*` | Unchanged in shape. | | CLI | `cawco artifact create --kind stage --file …`, per §5.10's rule. | **Panel** (the preview sheet's recipe, head title = the stage name; two floating groups per the Claude-panel reference): - **Starting:** "Starting Vite in `apps/dashboard`…" with elapsed seconds. Past 60 s → Error with the host's last stderr lines. - **Compiling:** a thin progress line in the head; the last render stays. - **Error:** over the dimmed last render: the message, `file:line:column`, the code frame. Clears on the next good compile. The agent already has it through delivery; no button needed. - **Live:** the render; top-left group = the variant strip (all, or one; from `data-cawco-variant`), top-right group = viewport widths; pins, ink, comments and picks as on any artifact. - **Asleep:** "Waking…" (Starting with a warm cache) on open. **What CawCo builds:** `packages/stage-host/` (`host.mjs`: launcher, the `cawcoStage()` plugin, mount table, shell builder, relay; vendored code-inspector core); daemon `stage-supervisor.ts` (spawn in the sandbox, health, restart, idle stop, event → hub); hub artifact store `kind: "stage"` with `status/errors/root/runtime` and error delivery; dashboard: the five states, variant strip, viewport group, the overlay's source reader, pin payload fields. **What it reuses:** the project's `vite` and framework plugin; Svelte 5's `__svelte_meta`; `code-inspector-plugin` (vendored; licence per the research report); the preview proxy, overlay, bridge, Yjs doc, pins/comments, `data-cawco-choice`. ## 6. Probes, in order (each: pass/fail; "stop and bring it" on fail — no fallback branch) 1. **SvelteKit under programmatic Vite.** From `apps/dashboard`, `host.mjs` serves `/__cawco/stage/src/lib/cawco/transcript/cards.stage.svelte` importing two real `transcript/*.svelte` components and `app.css`, through the hub proxy into the panel. Pass: renders with Tailwind and tokens applied, `$lib` and `$app/environment` resolve, an edit to the component shows in < 1 s without reload, Vite's HMR WebSocket works through the proxy. Note whether `$app/state`'s `page` throws outside kit's root (record it; a stage that needs it is the agent's problem to mock, not a shim CawCo ships). 2. **Source metadata.** On that render, five elements' `__svelte_meta.loc` match the source `file:line:column` (5/5), and the component chain names `EventCard`. 3. **Error loop.** Break the stage's syntax: the agent's delivery carries `{file, line, column, message}` within 3 s, the panel shows Error, the fix returns Live without reload. 4. **Lifecycle.** The host, spawned by the supervisor in the workspace sandbox, is alive 30 min after the session's last turn with the panel open; after `kill -9` the next open renders within the warm budget; idle stop and wake behave as §1.3. 5. **Runtime.** The same host runs under `node` and under `bun` for the dashboard (and with Vite 5, 6 and 7 if the research report lists projects on each). 6. **A second framework.** A Vue 3 (or React) Vite project renders a stage and a click maps to `file:line:column` through the vendored transform. ## 7. What would change this - If the research report shows code-inspector's Svelte 5 transform is unreliable: nothing changes for Svelte (`__svelte_meta` is used, not the transform). If its licence is not permissive or its Vue/React transforms are weak: source mapping for those frameworks is written per framework (Vue via its compiler's source positions; React 19 has no `_debugSource`, so React waits for a Babel transform of our own) and those frameworks move out of v1's claim. - If a compiled Bun binary can reliably `import()` an external file at runtime: run `host.mjs` with CawCo's own binary and drop the node/bun detection. - If probe 1 shows SvelteKit's catch-all swallows `/__cawco/*` or `$app/*` cannot be imported outside kit's root: bring it to the owner; the options then are an `appType: "custom"` server or a stage route under the app's own routes, both of which touch the project — a decision the owner makes. - If the preview proxy cannot carry Vite's HMR socket under a path prefix: set Vite's `base` per host to the proxy prefix, or proxy by host; probe 1 decides which. - If the owner wants person-side direct manipulation in v1 (the §3 pick), the overlay's edit-proposal pin moves into v1; the AST write-back stays out regardless. - If a `preview` of the whole app is what the agent reaches for anyway in practice, the stage still earns its keep for components; nothing here removes `preview`. Checks: - installed dependencies: bun install (bun.lock changed since the dependencies were installed) (0.6s) - no repo changes: pass (exit 0, 0.7s) Nothing pushed: this item lands none. Commits: ```` (none) ```` Diffstat: ```` (no changes) ```` Findings: 1. PRD D29 text says "no dev server for the agent to keep alive": §5.10 "Live components (D29)" reads as if no server exists. This spec keeps a server (the project's Vite) but moves its ownership to the daemon's supervisor. When D29 is updated, the wording should be "no server for the agent to keep alive" so it stays true. 2. The orchestrator's CSF view challenged: Composing with Storybook CSF needs the project to carry Storybook's renderer packages, which CawCo cannot install. The spec uses a plain component file in the project's framework as the composition format and leaves CSF as free interop for projects that already have Storybook. [Work item 8866317b-f4ce-4f81-963c-d30c15873afd is done in workspace f59bb492-1d83-4158-b2bd-bb3f8e30b0ce. A handoff to it continues this same session.]

Fable's spec is in. In short, CawCo compiles nothing itself:
1. **The stage file:** the agent writes a "stage" file in the project's own language that imports the real components and lays out variants on mock data.
2. **The project's own Vite:** CawCo's daemon runs the project's own Vite inside the workspace and keeps it alive (restart on crash, sleep when idle, wake on open), showing it through the existing preview proxy. CawCo installs nothing; it uses the project's own Vite and Node or Bun.

4. **Coverage:** v1 is any Vite project (Svelte/SvelteKit, Vue, React, Solid, Preact, Lit). Flutter, Expo and SwiftUI come later as their own hosts.
5. **Before any build:** six probes, starting with the real transcript cards in our own dashboard.

Revised live-components spec after reading the prior-art report whole. The finished item's report (the full spec) stands; the hub echoed the first version back on my second finish_item, so here is what the report changed, to apply over it.

CONFIRMED, NOT CHANGED — who compiles. The report's own findings back the spec: "Nothing renders arbitrary frameworks without running the user's own dev command"; "Every edit-to-source tool relies on a running Vite dev server for both the source mapping and the write endpoint"; Onlook's current desktop app "runs your app with your project's own dev command, and shows the running app in frames", with Claude Code editing the worktree. That is the spec's architecture: the project's own Vite, started programmatically by the daemon in the workspace, proxied like a preview. The report's closing "Fit for CawCo" recommends the opposite (a Bun.build plugin patterned on the Svelte REPL). I reject it on the report's own evidence: the REPL's aliases "map to virtual paths only, not to real directories"; it "fetches from npm/CDN at runtime"; "no single bundler plugin covers many frameworks", so it is "realistically Svelte first"; and it never sees the project's Vite config (Tailwind's Vite plugin, PostCSS, vitePreprocess, SvelteKit's $app/$env). The owner's requirement is every framework in the project's real context. A sketch with no project behind it is already the PRD's OpenUI mockup library (§5.7), so there is no case left for a second compiler. Owner's pick, recommended: project's own Vite; do not build the Bun.build path.

CHANGED 1 — pins carry two locations. From Onlook's instance-vs-definition mode ("edit this instance means edit the call site") and vite-plugin-svelte inspector commit 4158aa2 (walks __svelte_meta.parent "to jump to where a component is used"): a pin's payload is { definition: {file,line,column} (the element's own markup inside the component), instance: {file,line,column} (the call site in the stage or parent component, from the parent chain), component, variant }. The agent edits the component for all instances, the call site for a prop on this one. For JSX the vendored code-inspector transform "rewrites component roots to read props['data-insp-path']", which gives the instance.

CHANGED 2 — loc arithmetic and re-anchoring. __svelte_meta.loc is 0-based (the inspector adds 1 to both) and "goes stale after any edit and must be re-read from the DOM". The reader adds 1; for stage artifacts the pin's primary anchor is the element (selector, then text) and both locations are refreshed from the live DOM after every HMR `update` event. Pages keep the §5.7 order (file:line first). Desktop: the location link opens the editor through Vite's own /__open-in-editor on the host (the inspector's mechanism; own knowledge that Vite serves it; probe 2).

CHANGED 3 — how code-inspector is loaded. Report: "Not as shipped. There is no CLI, no bin, no zero-config mode"; a wrapper config is "our own untested idea". The host already calls createServer({ configFile: <project's>, plugins: [cawcoStage(), codeInspector(vendored)] }) — that is the wrapper made concrete without touching the project's files (Vite merges inline plugins with the config file's: own knowledge, probe 6). Transforms vendored into host.mjs (MIT, verified by the report; the JSX transform carries a Babel parser, so host.mjs is a few MB, measured in probe 6). The Svelte transform is not vendored: the report calls it "redundant" where __svelte_meta exists.

CHANGED 4 — Flutter. The report found `flutter widget-preview start` (official, "launches a local server and opens a real-time preview environment in your browser", @Preview annotations, read-only, API "not stable"). The Flutter host frames that server through the proxy instead of my `flutter run -d web-server` design; the stage is the framework's own @Preview file; no element-to-source exists there, so pins anchor to the preview function's file:line plus a selector; the host is pinned to a Flutter version range. SwiftUI and Compose confirmed IDE-bound → snapshot host as specced (add Compose @Preview composables to it). React Native: Storybook's react-native-web-vite proves the Vite path for RN-on-web where the project has a Vite config; native fidelity through the snapshot host.

CONFIRMED — CSF is not the format: addon-svelte-csf needs rollup's this.parse/this.getModuleInfo; composeStories is "a per-framework package"; "CSF is a de-facto standard, not a spec". A plain component file in the project's language needs none of that.

CONFIRMED — CawCo does not write source itself in v1: "Svelte has no Babel-equivalent that keeps formatting" ("Printing the AST again collapses the whitespace between nodes"); Glide's regex write-back "too fragile". If the owner later wants CawCo-side write-back (the §3 v2 pick), the method is stylewright's: svelte/compiler parse({modern:true}) offsets + magic-string splice, one implementation per framework; proposals grouped per file as Onlook groups requests.

PROBES, amended: 2 adds "+1 matches editor lines; the parent chain yields the stage call site; /__open-in-editor opens the file". 3 adds "pins keep their element and refresh their locations". 6 becomes "Vue 3 (or React) stage with the vendored transform loaded through createServer's inline plugins; tap maps to file:line:column; host.mjs size recorded". §7 adds: if probe 6 shows the vendored transforms cannot run outside code-inspector's plugin shell, write the Vue and JSX stamping ourselves (one transform each; the report shows the shape) and React waits until then.

Two things the report did not verify and the probes cover: whether Vite's inline plugins merge with a configFile under SvelteKit (probes 1/6), and whether code-inspector's transforms run outside its plugin shell (probe 6). Treat the report's closing paragraph as a view, not a finding.
