Headline: Rewritten around the Figma/pen/Paper model: a "design" artifact — a framework-neutral component tree with a small flex vocabulary bound to the project's tokens, stored in the artifact's Yjs doc, read and written by agents as HTML-shaped markup, rendered by CawCo itself on a pan-and-zoom canvas, edited by the person in place, ported to any framework by an agent as an ordinary task. It replaces the OpenUI mockup library; the Vite live-code idea is dropped.

# Designs (D29, rewritten) — the spec

Sources: PRD §5.7 (design systems, mockups), §5.10 (artifacts, tools, the Yjs doc), the decision log; the brief's evidence on pen.dev, Paper and Onlook. Claims from my own knowledge rather than a source are marked "(own knowledge)". No repo file beyond the PRD was read; nothing was written.

## 0. The answer in one paragraph

A **design** is a fourth artifact kind beside page, canvas and preview: a tree of frames, text, images, icons, component definitions, instances and slots, laid out with a small flex vocabulary and coloured, sized and typeset only by the project's token names. CawCo stores it in the artifact's Yjs doc, renders it to HTML/CSS itself (the same shadow-root host the mockup library uses today, with the project's token CSS and fonts), and shows it on a pan-and-zoom canvas with artboards. Agents read and write it as HTML-shaped markup through the artifact tools; the person edits it in place on the canvas (select, move, resize, text, spacing, colour, variant) and every edit is a Yjs transaction the agent sees. Code comes in the way pen.dev does it ("Ask the agent to read an existing component and recreate it on the canvas"): an agent reads the source and writes a definition. Code goes out the same way: an agent ports the design to Svelte, React, React Native, SwiftUI or Flutter as an ordinary coding task, and the port is traceable because every node has a stable id that the emitted code carries. This works for a pure-design project with no code and no toolchain, because nothing of the project runs: CawCo's own renderer draws the tree. The OpenUI mockup library is replaced by it; OpenUI stays only for live agent-made views (blocks, "Ask Caw for a view"), which need tools and data and are a different job. The Vite live-code host from the earlier spec is dropped; a project with code keeps `preview` for seeing real code run.

## 1. The format: a node tree with a flex vocabulary, written as markup

**Decision: a node tree (pen's shape), stored as nodes in the Yjs doc, serialised for agents and for files as HTML-shaped markup, rendered by CawCo to HTML/CSS.** Not raw HTML/CSS (Paper's), not OpenUI Lang extended.

Against the three tests:

- **Agents read and write it well.** The markup is HTML-shaped (tags, attributes, nesting), which agents write better than any JSON tree; pen's JSON works for agents because its MCP patches nodes by id, and this format keeps that too (every node has an id; edits are patches by id). A whole screen is one readable block; a change is one patch. The hub parses markup to the tree and back without loss, and a parse error comes back with its line.
- **Renders identically on the web, iPad and iPhone web views.** The vocabulary is a fixed subset that every WebKit and Blink engine lays out the same way: flexbox, fixed/hug/fill sizes, padding, gap, radius, stroke, fill, shadow, text styles (own knowledge that flexbox is stable across both engines; probe 1 pixel-diffs it). Fonts come from the project's `design/` assets, loaded by the renderer in every view, so no system-font drift. There is no project CSS, no arbitrary selectors, no user script: the same tree draws the same picture everywhere.
- **Ports cleanly to native targets.** Every node type has a direct equivalent in each target (the table in §4). Raw HTML/CSS fails this test: floats, grid, arbitrary selectors and cascade have no SwiftUI or Flutter form, so a port from Paper-style HTML is lossy. OpenUI Lang fails the first and third: it is an app-view language with queries and tools (PRD 2026-10-13: views' `Query()` tools; `@openuidev/lang-core` runtime), not a design document with definitions, instances, overrides and slots; adding those means forking a third-party 1.0 language, and porting from it needs its parser.

The markup, by example (the dashboard's event card, assembled):

```html
<design name="transcript-cards" tokens="design/tokens.css">
  <component id="EventCard" source="apps/dashboard/src/lib/cawco/transcript/EventCard.svelte"
             props="density: compact|roomy = compact; title: text; status: ok|error|running = ok">
    <frame id="c.root" layout="column" gap="{density == compact ? s1 : s2}" pad="{density == compact ? s2 : s3}"
           fill="surface" radius="r2" stroke="hairline">
      <frame id="c.head" layout="row" gap="s2" align="center">
        <icon id="c.icon" name="solar:terminal-bold-duotone" size="i4" color="ink-2"/>
        <text id="c.title" style="label" color="ink-1" lines="1">{title}</text>
        <instance id="c.badge" of="StatusDot" state="{status}"/>
      </frame>
      <slot id="c.body" name="body"/>
    </frame>
  </component>

  <artboard id="a1" name="Compact vs roomy" device="desktop" width="960">
    <frame id="a1.row" layout="row" gap="s4" pad="s4">
      <instance id="a1.c1" of="EventCard" density="compact" title="bun run build" status="ok" choice="density" option="compact">
        <text id="a1.c1.b" style="mono" color="ink-2">exit 0 · 2.1s</text>
      </instance>
      <instance id="a1.c2" of="EventCard" density="roomy" title="bun run build" status="error" choice="density" option="roomy">
        <text id="a1.c2.b" style="mono" color="ink-2">error TS2345 at src/x.ts:12</text>
        <override id="a1.c2.ov" node="c.title" color="danger"/>
      </instance>
    </frame>
    <note id="a1.n1" at="a1.c2">Roomy shows the full first line of the error.</note>
  </artboard>
</design>
```

**Node types:** `design` (root; names its token CSS), `component` (a definition: declared `props`, a single root frame, `source` when it came from code), `artboard` (a top-level frame with a device preset: phone, tablet, desktop, or free), `frame` (box; `layout` row|column|free, `gap`, `pad`, `align`, `justify`, `wrap`, `width`/`height` as fixed|hug|fill, `fill`, `stroke`, `radius`, `shadow`, `clip`, `scroll`, `hidden`), `text` (`style` token, `color` token, `align`, `lines` truncation, content), `image` (`asset` by name from `design/`, `fit`), `icon` (icon set name; CawCo's own is Solar duotone, kept per the house rule), `instance` (`of`, prop values, children fill the default slot, `slot=` on a child names another), `slot` (a named hole in a definition), `override` (a descendant override inside an instance: pen's `descendants`), `note` (an annotation, drawn on the canvas, never ported). Picks use the existing contract: `choice` and `option` on any node (D19). Prop expressions are limited to the one form shown: a prop reference, or a ternary on an enum prop. Nothing else computes.

**Values are token names**: colours, type styles, spacing (`s1…`), radii, shadows, icon sizes, from the project's `design/` system (§5.7) or, for a project without one, CawCo's neutral base set (never CawCo's own look, as the mockups rule says). A raw value (`fill="#334"`) is accepted and drawn, and shown as "untokened" in the inspector and in `artifact_read`, so the agent or the verifier session lifts it into a token. Nothing is silently rejected except an unknown component or token, refused by name, as the mockup library does today.

**Files.** The hub's Yjs doc is the truth while the design is worked on; `artifact_promote` writes the markup to `design/<name>.design.html` (readable in git, diffable per node line) and each `component` in it to `design/components/<Name>.design.html`, which is the project's component library. Ids are stable across promote, read and update: the hub assigns an id to any node written without one and returns the markup with ids filled in (D25's rule for canvas elements).

## 2. The component model

- **Definition** (`component`): a named tree with declared props. Prop types: `text`, `number`, `bool`, an enum (`a|b|c`), a token type (`color`, `space`, `style`), `image`, and `slot`. Each has a default. Enum props are the variants: `density: compact|roomy` is what Figma calls a variant property (own knowledge of Figma's model). A definition may use instances of other definitions.
- **Instance** (`instance of=`): renders the definition with the given prop values; unspecified props take defaults. Children fill the default slot; `slot="name"` on a child fills a named one.
- **Override** (`override node=`): changes one property of one descendant of this instance (text, colour, hidden, an icon name), by the definition's node id. Everything not overridden follows the definition, so editing the definition updates every instance. "Detach" copies the definition's tree into the instance's place and drops the link.
- **Slots**: holes in a definition, filled per instance; a definition's `slot` may carry placeholder children drawn when empty.
- **Tokens**: a definition's colours, spacing and type styles are token names, so the same definition draws correctly in any project that has those roles, and a port emits token references, not literals. The renderer loads the project's token CSS and fonts into the shadow root (the mockup library's mechanism, kept).
- **Library**: the project's `design/components/` plus CawCo's base definitions (button, input, toggle, checkbox, select, tabs, dialog drawn open, toast, list row, avatar, badge, the device frames: the mockup primitives' list, re-expressed as definitions). The hub builds the library and the agent's prompt from it by content hash, as `mockups.ts` does today for OpenUI; `generateSystemPrompt`'s role moves to `design-library.ts`. CawCo's own dashboard components stop being a `system: "cawco"` switch and become imported definitions in the cockpit repo's `design/components/` (§4).

## 3. Editing

**The person, on the canvas.** The surface is CawCo's own pan-and-zoom (a transformed container; pinch and two-finger pan on iPad, wheel and drag on the desk; no library — Excalidraw does not do flex layout or DOM children, and Penpot is a whole application, MPL-licensed, not an embeddable kernel (own knowledge)). Artboards sit on it; the rest is the browser's flexbox doing the layout.

- **Select**: tap selects the topmost node under the pointer at the artboard level; tap again goes into the instance or frame (Figma's depth model, own knowledge); Esc goes up. The selection shows its id, type and, for an instance, its definition.
- **Move**: dragging inside a flex frame reorders among siblings (an insertion line shows the index); dragging into a `free` frame or artboard sets `x`/`y`; arrow keys nudge by one spacing step. Drag out of a frame to re-parent.
- **Resize**: handles set `width`/`height` to a fixed value; the inspector switches fixed, hug, fill.
- **Text**: double-tap edits in place; the content writes to the node, or to an `override` when the text is inside an instance.
- **Spacing and colour**: the inspector (right panel on wide screens, bottom sheet on phones) steps `pad`, `gap`, `radius` through the token scale and picks `fill`, `stroke`, `color` from the project's tokens; a raw value field exists and marks the node untokened.
- **Variant**: the inspector shows the instance's enum props as segmented controls; changing one is a prop write. Swap instance to another definition; reset an override; detach.
- **Undo**: `Y.UndoManager` scoped to the person's own transactions (own knowledge of Yjs).
- **Pins, comments, picks, ink**: as on every artifact, but anchored by node id, which is stable across edits — better than selectors, so the "moved" tray is rarely used. Picks keep `choice`/`option`.

Every edit is one Yjs transaction on the node, so the agent, the iPad and a second tab converge, and nothing moves under a hand (the pointer-up rule of §5.10 holds).

**The agent, through tools** (names from §5.10; `writing-for-agents` writes the descriptions):

| Tool | For a design |
|---|---|
| `artifact_create` | `kind: "design"`, `name`, `markup`. Answers the id, the route, and the markup with ids assigned; refuses an unknown component or token by name; a parse error comes with its line. |
| `artifact_update` | `markup` replaces the document **merged by node id** (a node with the same id is updated in place, so selection, pins and the person's unsent edits survive; the tree's idiomorph), or `patch`: operations by node id — `set` a prop, `insert` markup under a parent at an index, `move`, `delete`, `override`. Answers the markup after the change and every node the person changed since the agent's last read, flagged (D23's rule). |
| `artifact_read` | The markup with ids, the untokened nodes, pins, comments, picks, and `changed` since a cursor; `png: true` renders the artboards (the renderer draws to a canvas element in the viewer; without a viewer, the hub's headless render — probe 4 decides whether that is the dashboard's own renderer in a worker or a browser on the hub). |
| `artifact_show`, `artifact_promote`, `comment_*` | Unchanged. Promote writes the files of §1. |
| `design_library` | Reads the project's definitions with their props, for a session that is about to write a design. |

The person's edits reach the agent as today: batched after 3 s of quiet, at once during the agent's turn, and "Send N" for pins and picks.

## 4. Import and port

**Import (code → canvas), pen's way.** An agent reads a component's source in any framework and writes a `component` definition with the same prop names, the same variant values, tokens by role, and `source="<path>"` plus `source-hash` on the definition. No project toolchain runs. The orchestrator dispatches it as a brief: "read these files, write these definitions, prove by rendering the design and comparing with the app's screenshot through the verifier session (§5.7)". Later, when a project has code and the owner asks for parity, a re-import diffs the new definition against the stored one and shows the changed nodes.

**Port (canvas → code, any target).** An ordinary coding task from the design's markup, guided by a CawCo-written `port-design` skill (D14) that carries the mapping:

| Node | Web (Svelte/React) | React Native | SwiftUI | Flutter |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `frame` row/column | flex div | `View` with flexDirection | `HStack`/`VStack` (+ `Spacer` for `fill`) | `Row`/`Column` (+ `Expanded`) |
| `frame` free | relative + absolute children | absolute children | `ZStack` + `.position` | `Stack` + `Positioned` |
| `text` | element with the style class | `Text` with the style | `Text` + `.font` | `Text` + `TextStyle` |
| `image`/`icon` | `img`/icon component | `Image`/icon | `Image`/`AsyncImage` | `Image`/`Icon` |
| `component` + `instance` | a component and its use | same | a `View` struct and its use | a widget and its use |
| `slot` | children / Snippet | `children` | `@ViewBuilder` closure | a `Widget` parameter |
| tokens | the token CSS | a tokens module | `Color`/`Font` extensions from the tokens | a `ThemeData`/tokens class |
| `note`, `choice`, untokened marks | not ported | | | |

**Traceability.** Every emitted component carries its origin (`<!-- design: transcript-cards#EventCard -->` or the language's comment form, and on web roots `data-design="EventCard"`), and the port writes back to the design: `ported="svelte: apps/dashboard/src/lib/.../EventCard.svelte @ <commit>"` on the definition. After that, a pin on the design names the file, and `artifact_read(since: <the port's cursor>)` lists exactly the nodes changed since the port, which is the next port's work list. A port to a second target adds a second `ported` entry; the design stays the one source.

## 5. The Vite live-code idea

Dropped. A project with code sees its real code through the existing `preview` (a dev server or folder); nothing in this feature runs the project.

## 6. What this replaces and keeps (one mechanism per job)

- **Replaced:** the OpenUI mockup library (`@cawco/core/mockups`, hub `mockups.ts`, `views/openui/mockup`, the `system: "cawco"` switch, the specimen templates with `{{prop}}` holes). Its jobs move into designs: primitives become base definitions, specimens become imported definitions, the shadow-root host and token CSS loading are kept as the design renderer's host. Cutover, not alongside (change rule 1).
- **Kept:** OpenUI for live agent-made views with data (blocks, "Ask Caw for a view"), which a design does not do. `page` for decision pages and forms. `canvas` (Excalidraw) for drawing; ink on any artifact. `preview` for running code. The Yjs doc, pins, comments, picks, dials, delivery, the panel and its states.
- **Later, and what triggers it:** Script nodes (pen's live `.js` layers) when the owner asks for motion or data in a design; parity checks (import diff) when a project with code asks; a second port target's skill when the first project needs it.

## 7. Worked example: the transcript cards, as it would have gone

Import `EventCard.svelte` and `StatusDot.svelte` as definitions (one brief, no server). On an artboard, two instances with `density` as a `choice`; a third artboard with the error state. The owner picks on the iPad and drops a pin on the roomy title ("heavier"); the agent reads the flagged nodes, sets `style="label-strong"` on `c.title`, the canvas updates in place. Port the picked definition back to `EventCard.svelte` with the origin comment. Zero lines of throwaway dev-route code.

## 8. What must be proven first

1. **Render and parity.** Three dashboard components imported as definitions; the same design rendered in Chrome and in the iPad web view; pixel diff under the probe kit's threshold on the artboards. Pass: < 0.5 % differing pixels, all in text antialiasing. Fail: the vocabulary or the renderer has an engine-dependent feature; remove it.
2. **Agents write it.** Five screens of the dashboard written as markup by a Sonnet and an Opus session from the generated prompt. Pass: ≤ 1 parse error per screen, each fixed from the error line on the next call; no unknown-component refusals except real ones.
3. **Person ↔ agent round trip.** On the iPad: move, text edit, variant swap, pin. Pass: `artifact_read` returns the four nodes flagged within 3 s of quiet; an `artifact_update` with full markup keeps the person's selection and pins.
4. **Headless render.** `artifact_read(png: true)` with no viewer attached, from the hub. Pass: a PNG per artboard within 2 s; the probe records which mechanism it took.
5. **Port and trace.** The picked definition ported to Svelte by an Opus leaf with the skill; build, lint, type-check green; the origin comment present; `ported` written on the definition; `artifact_read(since)` after one more edit lists only that node.

## 9. What would change this

- If probe 1 fails on a feature the owner wants (blur, glass), that feature becomes a `note`d intent ported by hand rather than a rendered property.
- If probe 2 shows agents fight the markup, the tools accept the same tree as JSON too (pen's form); the tree is unchanged.
- If the owner wants designs to feel live (hover, press), enum props named `state` get a canvas toggle; still no script.
- If a project needs a design to show its real component rather than a recreation, that is `preview`, and the earlier Vite host would be the way to make it precise; it is not built unless he asks.

# A Protocol for Agent-Driven Interfaces¶

 A2UI enables AI agents to generate rich, interactive user interfaces that render natively across web, mobile, and desktop—without executing arbitrary code.
...
Instead of text-only responses or risky code execution, A2UI lets agents send declarative component descriptions that clients render using their own native widgets. It's like having agents speak a universal UI language.
...
- A2UI specifications (v0.9.1 current, v1.0 candidate).
- Implementations for renderers (Angular, Flutter, Lit, Markdown, etc.) on the client side.
- Transports like A2A which communicate A2UI messages between agents and clients.

- Secure by Design
...
Declarative data format, not executable code. Agents can only use pre-approved components from your catalog—no UI injection attacks.
...
Flat, streaming JSON structure designed for easy generation. LLMs can build UIs incrementally without perfect JSON in one shot.
- Framework-Agnostic
...
One agent response works everywhere. Render the same UI on Angular, Flutter, React, or native mobile with your own styled components.
...
1. User sends a message to an AI agent
2. Agent generates A2UI messages describing the UI (structure + data)
3. Messages stream to the client application
4. Client renders using native components (Angular, Flutter, React, etc.)
5. User interacts with the UI, sending actions back to the agent
6. Agent responds with updated A2UI messages

Title: A2UI v0.9: The New Standard for Portable, Framework ...

Author: Google A2UI Team
Highlights:
Generative UI allows AI agents to generate tailored UI widgets in real-time, matching the interface to the user’s specific interaction. But to move from demos to production, we need a clean separation of concerns. A2UI v0.9 is our answer; a framework-agnostic standard for declaring UI intent. It allows local or remote agents to communicate with any client application using a common language, ensuring your agent can generate your UI using your existing component catalog on any device.
...
- From "Standard" to "Basic": Frontend developers don't want new components. They already have a design system and components they use. Agents should respond dynamically, using existing front ends. We renamed our optional component set to 'Basic' to make this more clear. Check out the component catalog docs and code samples, connect A2UI to your awesome front ends.
- A Shared Web-Core Library: On the client side, we've introduced a shared web-core library which vastly simplifies any browser UI renderer. We've also landed the official React renderer and version-bumped all A2UI supported renderers (Flutter, Lit, Angular, and React), while carving out a dedicated spot for community renderers.
...
- AG-UI: Support for connecting a broad spectrum of GenUI capabilities into agentic web apps, including A2UI, MCP Apps and Open Generative UI.
...
Any agent that already speaks AG-UI can drive A2UI v0.9 on day zero. No custom integration is required. This works through AG-UI's middleware system: a small piece of code that plugs into your existing agent pipeline. It teaches your agent how to speak A2UI, wires the responses correctly, and handles streaming, converting the agent's output into components your UI can render immediately, using A2UI's built-in renderers or your own custom components.

Diez is an open-source developer toolkit for building & maintaining design tokens at scale.

Write & maintain styles in one place, then compile & consume them everywhere:  Diez supports any UI component library or codebase written in Swift, Objective-C, Kotlin, Java, TypeScript, JavaScript/JSON, CSS, or SCSS.
...
Diez's toolkit comes in four parts:

 - **Compiler** — Diez includes a novel open-source compiler that converts (transpiles) TypeScript tokens into native packages for iOS, Android, and Web.

 

 - **Framework** — Diez's framework is a library of common design token patterns, including pre-written _prefabs_ for Typography, Colors, Images, Drop Shadows, Dimensions, and more. Prefabs can be configured, nested, and reused to express any style, brand, or theme you can imagine.

 

 You can also write your own custom prefabs. Open-source contributions welcome!

 - **Extractors** — Diez's extractors automate the retrieval of design tokens from Figma, Sketch, Adobe XD, and InVision DSM. These command-line utilities are powerful tools for customizing your own design/developer hand-offs and are a great fit for CI servers.

 

- **Documentation Generator** — Diez DocsGen builds customizable static HTML docs from any Diez project, complete with markdown-rendered code comments. Technically implemented as an additional compiler target, Diez DocsGen helps keep your styleguide and documentation perfectly up-to-date with your design token source of truth.
 
 **See an example Diez project and its DocsGen output.**

...
Think of design tokens as "design data": concepts like colors, typography definitions, spacings, sizings, and drop shadows — agnostic of any particular design tool or programming language. Design tokens are the basic building blocks that allow you to express any design language as pure data.

The magic of design tokens is they sit right at the gap between design and code — they're design concepts, but since they have no opinions about rendering or technologies, they're adaptable into any codebase with the right tooling (like Diez's cross-platform native compiler).

Design tokens are a community movement and the creators of Diez are actively contributing to the emerging W3C Design Tokens Community Group and specification.
...
- **Hierarchy, branding, and theming:** Real-world design systems often encompass multiple products, brands, and themes. In the ideal world, your team could maintain a core set of shared values, then extend and override them hierarchically for different layers of your "brand tree." Thanks to imports, exports, and native code reuse in TypeScript, this is completely doable. *Our team is also hard at work on a first-class Theming solution within Diez, which makes this set of functionality quicker & easier to manage.*

 - **Stability & scale:** TypeScript was designed for exactly this. Design tokens are especially fragile because of how they touch multiple codebases and platforms. Thanks to static typing, typedefs & comments that transpile all the way to iOS and Android, and developer-delighting features like autocomplete popovers — your team can evolve tokens reliably & confidently.

# Design Tokens specification reaches first stable version

 Kaelig Deloumeau-Prigent | Posted on: October 28, 2025
...
San Francisco, CA – October 28, 2025 – The Design Tokens Community Group today announced the first stable version of the Design Tokens Specification (2025.10), marking a milestone for design systems teams and tool makers worldwide. After years of collaborative development, the specification provides a production-ready, vendor-neutral format for sharing design decisions across tools and platforms.

Design tokens: the single source of truth for colors, typography, spacing, and other design decisions – have long been fragmented across proprietary formats. Teams maintaining multi-brand design systems often juggle dozens or even hundreds of token files manually, leading to drift, errors, and maintenance overhead. The new stable specification addresses this through standardized support for theming, modern color spaces, and cross-tool interoperability.
...
## What’s new in 2025.10

The stable specification introduces critical capabilities for scaling design systems:

- Theming and multi-brand support – manage light/dark modes, accessibility variants, and brand themes without file duplication
- Modern color specification – full support for Display P3, Oklch, and all CSS Color Module 4 spaces, matching how design tools actually work
- Rich token relationships – inheritance, aliases, and component-level references for sophisticated design systems
- Cross-platform consistency – one token file generates platform-specific code for iOS, Android, web, and Flutter
...
The specification’s stability is backed by reference implementations in leading tools including Style Dictionary, Tokens Studio, and Terrazzo. More than 10 design tools and open-source projects – including Penpot, Figma, Sketch, Framer, Knapsack, Supernova, and zeroheight – already support or are implementing the standard.
...
Developed by the Design Tokens Community Group, the specification reflects real-world use cases from design systems teams at companies of all sizes. The open standard ensures no single vendor controls the format, giving teams freedom to choose the best tools without compatibility concerns.
...
For design systems teams: Start exporting tokens in the stable format and provide feedback in the GitHub issues: https://github.com/design-tokens/community-group/issues.

For tool makers: Implement the specification to tap into an ecosystem of interoperable design tools. Full documentation, examples, and implementation guidance are available at designtokens.org.

# Penpot's Official MCP Server

Penpot integrates a LLM layer built on the Model Context Protocol
(MCP) via Penpot's Plugin API to interact with a Penpot design
file. Penpot's MCP server enables LLMs to perform data queries,
transformation and creation operations.

Penpot's MCP Server is unlike any other you've seen. You get
design-to- design, code-to-design and design-code supercharged

...
The **Penpot MCP Server** exposes tools to AI clients (LLMs), which
support the retrieval of design data as well as the modification and
creation of design elements. The MCP server communicates with Penpot
via the dedicated **Penpot MCP Plugin**,
which connects to the MCP server via WebSocket.

[Important update, Dec 4th 2025] We released a first version of our MCP Server. Feel free to browse this folder with raw footage. At least a dozen videos showcase different scenarios. My favourite ones are 03, 04, 06, 08 and 12.
...
### The good: Agentic AI and MCP servers
...
What is particularly interesting is how easy MCPs seem to make your app capabilities available through this new genAI-friendly API. If you have a well-documented traditional API, you can easily build your own MCP server and let any AI agent connect to it and operate really quickly and autonomously.
...
#### The Penpot way: Design Tokens to bring intent to design
...
Thankfully, we have Design Tokens. They represent small design decisions encapsulated in tiny bits of code that you can use, reuse and combine to create more intentional design decisions. A design token can be as obvious as a color, but it could also be a border radius or an opacity. There are many design token types but most complex designs will usually use just a dozen. For instance, you can define a spacing design token (ie: padding) as three times a dimension design token that is also referenced across a whole multi-brand identity theme. Changing a design token has automatic ripple effects. That is why some people have referred to this as parametric design. Whatever you call it, it unlocks true adaptative UIs.
...
The good news: they are all expressed canonically as code thanks to a W3C DTCG draft standard. It took a lot of courage two years ago, when we started this journey with the folks at Tokens Studio, but today Penpot is the only UI Design tool to support Design Tokens natively. The even better news: LLMs couldn’t have dreamt of an easier way to identify the design decisions that are invariant to an iterative design process.
...
Declarative design principles brought Penpot a rules-based visual language inspired by CSS. Design Systems and Design Tokens brought us scalable semantic design structures. Finally, our own open .penpot format means that every Penpot file is a zip file full of JSON files and visual assets. If we really want to build the next era of software building, we need to see both design and code as equally important. Hence our “Design as Code” motto.
...
### Penpot MCP Servers so that our community unlocks the platform’s true potential
...
With our enthusiastic community, at Penpot we have a better chance than anyone else to discover how and where LLM can best help the design process. This is why we have decided to provide an official Penpot MCP server to give everyone the ability to interact with a powerful and reliable design source of truth in ways we can’t even imagine at this time.

One example of what an Penpot MCP server of the calibre we're envisaging could unlock would be to make it easier to channel back production data about how your software is being used. From the simplest A/B test to more nuanced insights, this could allow an AI agent to surgically refactor bits of a design ... to better accommodate it to relevant emerging scenarios. Data and heuristics encourage a bolder ... process and we want our Penpot MCP server to unlock a full-duplex design-production communication.

In this sense, it’s crucial that our MCP server exposes our design primitives, plugins API, declarative design options, design system capabilities, design tokens and semantic inference aids in a way that you can really speak the “design’s code”. We’ll provide the most configurable MCP server we can, so that you don’t need to create one (and support you if you still want to).
...
### Penpot .penpot open format

Did you know that when you download a Penpot file using the .penpot format, you are downloading everything in a zipped file containing folders, JSON files and visual assets (SVGs, JPEGs, etc)?
...
This was released with Penpot 2.4 in January 2025 and though its potential wasn’t immediately made obvious, more and more people are starting to see the .penpot file format as the Penpot’s file-based API.

Two features in the works will allow for changes made in your local file-system to update the original Penpot instance file. With persistent universal references, updates will naturally cascade out to dependent files. This opens up the possibility to git-version designs (e.g. together with synced code), and seamlessly switch back and forth between sophisticated visual edits in Penpot and local text-based powertools (AI or AI-less).

With Penpot, you should be able to choose the best tool for the job, just as you can self-host it or use our SaaS.

Next, we show a Penpot component library where we want to modify a couple of properties for a button component as well as library-wide typographies. We download that file as a .penpot file, edit a bunch of internal JSON files and re-upload it using the API. Penpot makes sure to preserve inter-file dependencies so that a design using the modified library is also updated.

## Live components: what exists, and the options

**Facts I've checked:**
- **pen.dev:** renders its own `.pen` JSON. Code components get recreated by the agent ("Ask the agent to read an existing component and recreate it on the canvas"). Proprietary.
- **Paper:** its canvas is plain HTML/CSS. Using your real code components is on its roadmap, not shipped, and React only. Proprietary.
- **Penpot:** open-source design tool, self-hosted or SaaS (github.com/penpot/penpot).
  - It "works with open standards like SVG, CSS, HTML, and JSON".
  - Its `.penpot` file is "a zip file full of JSON files and visual assets".
  - It has native components, variants and design tokens.
  - It has an official, free MCP server for agents ("design-to-design, code-to-design and design-code"), run locally or hosted.
  - Catch: that MCP works through a Penpot tab with its plugin connected.
- **Design tokens have a standard:** W3C Design Tokens Community Group format 2025.10, "the first stable version". It's supported by Penpot, Figma, Sketch, Framer and Style Dictionary, and generates "platform-specific code for iOS, Android, web, and Flutter".
- **A2UI:** Google's open protocol (Apache-2.0) for "agents to generate … interfaces that render natively". Agents compose screens from your own component catalog. Its React, Lit, Angular and Flutter renderers are stable; SwiftUI and React Native renderers come from the community. We used A2UI before you switched us to OpenUI on 13 Oct.
- **Mitosis:** write a component once and compile it to React, Vue, Svelte, Angular, Solid, React Native and web components. But you write it in JSX.
- **Rendering a project's real code components** needs that project's own compiler. The Svelte team says compiling in the browser is "rather involved and also slow".

**The options:**

| | What it is | Rewrites components? | Pure-design projects | All frameworks | What CawCo builds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Penpot as the design surface** | Agents design in Penpot through its MCP; CawCo shows the Penpot file in the artifact panel; tokens in the W3C format | Code components must be recreated in Penpot once, and then live in two places | Yes | Design is framework-neutral; agents port it to any framework | Bringing up the user's Penpot (or hosting one), panel embedding, wiring its MCP into sessions |
| **B. Bring your own design tool** (Penpot, Figma, pen.dev, Paper over their MCP) | What your PRD already decided in D18: "No adapters … a session uses one as a project MCP server" | Same as A | Yes | Same as A | Almost nothing: MCP config, and showing their exports in the panel |
| **C. Real code components** | The agent writes a file that composes your real components; CawCo runs the project's own dev server and shows it; a click maps to the source line | **No.** One component, everything else is an instance | No: there's no code to run | Any framework with a supported toolchain, starting with Vite; native stacks get snapshots | A supervisor for the dev server, the panel, click-to-source |
| **D. Agents compose from a catalog** (A2UI, or the OpenUI we have) | Agents assemble screens from the project's component catalog; a renderer per platform draws the real components | No, but every catalog component needs an implementation in each renderer | No | Wherever a renderer exists | Mostly built (OpenUI), or a switch back to A2UI |

**My recommendation, for you to judge:**
- **C for projects that have code.** It's the only option that never rewrites a component, which is the defect you're trying to kill.
- **For design-only work, A or B.** Pick B (your own D18) unless you want CawCo to ship a design tool itself; then A (Penpot) is the open, standards-based one.
- **Tokens in the W3C format either way,** so design and code share one source.
- **D stays what it is today:** agent-made views, not a design tool.

**Not yet verified, if you want any of it checked before choosing:**
- Penpot's licence and how heavy self-hosting is.
- Whether Penpot's canvas can be embedded in our panel.
- What Figma's MCP can write back.
- How C behaves for frameworks that don't use Vite (Next, Angular).

Headline: Merged spec under one invariant: a component exists once and the canvas holds only instances. One design document and one component contract for both cases; a design-backed component is drawn by CawCo's renderer from its tree, a code-backed one is mounted from its real file by the project's own toolchain run by the daemon, and the handover from design to code is a one-time port gated by a parity render and an override-to-prop check, after which the tree body is deleted and the instances keep working unchanged.

# Designs and live components (D29, merged) — the spec

Sources: PRD §5.7, §5.10, decision log; the brief's evidence (pen.dev, Paper, Onlook, Svelte 5's `__svelte_meta`, code-inspector, Vite). Own-knowledge claims are marked "(own knowledge; probe N)". Nothing beyond the PRD read; nothing written.

## 0. The invariant and the answer

**A component exists exactly once. Everything on the canvas is an instance of it.** Nothing is re-coded per variant, per screen, per import, or per render.

A **design** is an artifact: a tree of artboards, frames, text, images, icons, instances, slots and notes, laid out with a small flex vocabulary and coloured, sized and typeset by the project's token names. Every `instance` points at one component. A component is one record in the project's library with a name, typed props (enums are the variants), named slots, and **one body**: either a **design body** (a tree in CawCo's neutral medium, for a project before it has code) or a **code body** (the real file in the project, for a project with code). The canvas, the pins, the tools and the person's editing see only the contract (name, props, slots, ids); which body a component has decides only *who draws it*: CawCo's renderer expands a design body; the project's own toolchain, run by the daemon inside the workspace, mounts a code body with the instance's props. When a project writes code for a design-backed component, that is a one-time port of the body; the record switches to `code=`, the tree body is deleted, and the instances do not change. Existing code is never recreated on the canvas: the file is the component, and the library record for it is a signature, not a copy.

## 1. The document: one tree, written as markup

Decision from the second spec, unchanged: a node tree stored in the artifact's Yjs doc (`nodes`), serialised for agents and for files as HTML-shaped markup with stable node ids, rendered by CawCo to HTML/CSS. Why: agents write HTML-shaped markup best and patch by id precisely (pen's MCP shape); a fixed flex vocabulary draws the same in every WebKit and Blink web view (own knowledge; probe 1); every node type has a direct SwiftUI, Flutter, React Native and web form, which raw HTML/CSS does not; OpenUI Lang is an app-view language with queries and tools, not a design document.

Node types: `design` (root; `tokens=` names the token CSS), `artboard` (device preset phone|tablet|desktop|free, width), `frame` (`layout` row|column|free, `gap`, `pad`, `align`, `justify`, `wrap`, `width`/`height` fixed|hug|fill, `fill`, `stroke`, `radius`, `shadow`, `clip`, `scroll`, `hidden`), `text` (`style`, `color`, `align`, `lines`, content), `image` (`asset`, `fit`), `icon` (set name; CawCo's own is Solar duotone), `instance` (`of`, prop values, children fill the default slot, `slot=` names another), `slot` (a named hole inside a design body), `override` (design-backed only, §2), `note` (annotation, never ported). `choice`/`option` on any node for picks (D19). Values are token names from `design/` (or CawCo's neutral base set for a project without one); a raw value is drawn and marked "untokened". Unknown component or token: refused by name (the mockup library's rule, kept). The hub assigns ids to nodes written without one and answers the markup with ids filled in (D25's rule).

Example, a code project:

```html
<design name="transcript-cards" tokens="apps/dashboard/src/lib/tokens/tokens.css">
  <artboard id="a1" name="Density" device="desktop" width="960">
    <frame id="a1.row" layout="row" gap="s4" pad="s4">
      <instance id="a1.c1" of="EventCard" density="compact" event="fixture:./cards.fixtures.ts#toolCall"
                choice="density" option="compact"/>
      <instance id="a1.c2" of="EventCard" density="roomy" event="fixture:./cards.fixtures.ts#failed"
                choice="density" option="roomy">
        <text id="a1.c2.b" slot="footer" style="mono" color="ink-2">error TS2345 at src/x.ts:12</text>
      </instance>
    </frame>
    <note id="a1.n1" at="a1.c2">Roomy shows the error's first line in full.</note>
  </artboard>
</design>
```

Files: the Yjs doc is the truth while the design is worked on; `artifact_promote` writes `design/<name>.design.html`. The library is `design/components/<Name>.design.html`, one file per component record (§2).

## 2. The component contract (one model, two bodies)

A **component record**:

```html
<component id="EventCard"
           props="density: compact|roomy = compact; event: json; status: ok|error|running = ok"
           slots="footer"
           code="apps/dashboard/src/lib/cawco/transcript/EventCard.svelte"/>
```

or, before code exists:

```html
<component id="Button" props="kind: primary|secondary|ghost = primary; label: text; disabled: bool = false" slots="leading">
  <frame id="b.root" layout="row" gap="s1" pad="s2 s3" fill="{kind == primary ? accent : surface}" radius="r2">
    <slot id="b.lead" name="leading"/>
    <text id="b.label" style="label" color="{kind == primary ? on-accent : ink-1}">{label}</text>
  </frame>
</component>
```

- **Props**: `text`, `number`, `bool`, enum (`a|b|c` — the variants, Figma's variant properties (own knowledge)), token types (`color`, `space`, `style`), `image`, `json`. Each has a default. A `json` or any prop may take `fixture:<path>#<export>`, a value imported from a project file by the host (code projects only).
- **Slots**: named holes; an instance's children fill them. A design body declares them with `slot` nodes; a code body's slots are the file's children/snippets/`@ViewBuilder`s, named in `slots=`.
- **Instance**: `of`, prop values (unspecified → defaults), slot children. Editing the component changes every instance; there is no copy anywhere.
- **Override** (`override node= prop= value=`): allowed only on an instance of a **design-backed** component, addressing a descendant node of its body (pen's `descendants`). A code body has no addressable inner nodes, so its variation is props and slots only. This asymmetry is what makes the handover (§4) a defined step rather than a leak.
- **Body**: `design` (the tree inside the record) or `code` (`code=` path; the framework is read from the file's extension and the Vite root's `package.json`). Exactly one; never both. Nothing in the contract names the body except `code=`.
- **Library**: `design/components/*` plus CawCo's base records (button, input, toggle, checkbox, select, tabs, dialog, toast, list row, avatar, badge, device frames: the mockup primitives, as design bodies). The hub builds the library and the agent's prompt from it by content hash (the `mockups.ts` mechanism, moved to `design-library.ts`). For a code project, a record with `code=` is **declared**, not copied: an agent reads the file's props and writes the signature line — the same as a `.d.ts` or Storybook's argTypes, with none of the body. Later: the host derives the signature from the file where the framework exposes it (Svelte's `$props()` type, Vue's `defineProps`, React's TS props), triggered when the owner wants declarations to stop being manual.

The record switches body exactly once in its life, design → code (§4). It never goes back: once code exists, the file is the component.

## 3. Rendering: one renderer, two mount paths, the venue follows the components

The renderer is one framework-free script, shipped in the overlay (which already runs inside the shadow-root host and inside every preview iframe). It walks the tree and draws frames, text, images, icons and notes to DOM with the token CSS and fonts loaded. For an `instance` it does one of two things:

- **Design-backed**: expands the body with the instance's props and overrides, recursively. Pure DOM; no project code.
- **Code-backed**: leaves a mount point carrying the props and asks the **stage host** to mount the real file into it.

**Venue.** A project with no code renders in the dashboard's shadow-root host (the mockup library's, kept) — always live, nothing to start. A project with code renders at `/__cawco/design/<artifact-id>` on the stage host, so the project's framework, modules, token CSS and fonts are present; the same renderer script runs there under the overlay.

**The stage host** (the first spec, kept whole; condensed here): the daemon on the workspace's machine runs the project's own Vite programmatically from the workspace's own `node_modules` (`createServer({ configFile: <project's>, plugins: [cawcoDesign(), ...] })`; inline plugins merge with the config file's: own knowledge, probe 2), with the runtime the project's lockfile implies (`bun` or `node`), inside the workspace sandbox, as a listener the supervisor owns: start on first use, `ready` within 60 s, health every 15 s, restart ×3 with backoff then `error`, asleep after 30 min idle, wake on open, stop on archive. One embedded `host.mjs` in CawCo's binary, written to `.cawco/stage/` (git-excluded); nothing installed into the project; refused by name if no Vite root, no `vite`, or no runtime. Our plugin serves the design page (an HTML shell from the app's own `app.html`/`index.html`), a virtual module `cawco:mount?components=EventCard,StatusDot` that imports each code-backed component's file and the fixtures the instances name, an event relay (`ready`, `update`, `error {file,line,column,message,frame}`, `clear`) on stdout, and, for frameworks without dev metadata, the vendored code-inspector transforms (MIT per the research report). Vite's error overlay is off; ours shows.

**Mount adapters** (the only per-framework code, inside `host.mjs`): Svelte `mount(Component, { target, props })`; Vue `createApp`; React `createRoot`; Solid `render`; Preact `render`. **Slots**: the instance's slot children are neutral nodes the renderer draws; the adapter passes them as the framework's children: Svelte through `createRawSnippet` rendering a placeholder the renderer then fills (own knowledge that Svelte 5 exports `createRawSnippet`; probe 3); React as a `children` element holding a ref'd container; Vue as a render-function slot. **HMR**: the adapter accepts module updates and re-mounts the affected instances with the same props (`import.meta.hot.accept`, own knowledge; probe 2), so editing the real file re-draws every instance in place, state of the rest of the canvas untouched. **Props** that cross from the tree to the component are JSON, token names (passed as the token's string), or fixture exports.

Panel states for a code project: Starting ("Starting Vite in `apps/dashboard`…"), Compiling (progress line, last render stays), Error (message, `file:line:column`, frame, over the dimmed render; also delivered to the agent within 3 s), Live, Asleep ("Waking…"). A no-code design has only Live.

## 4. The one-time handover: design body → code body

Trigger: the project starts writing code, or the owner says "build this". An agent (an ordinary coding task, guided by the `port-design` skill, D14) writes the component's code **once** from the design body, keeping the contract: same name, same prop names and enum values, same slot names, tokens by role. The emitted file carries its origin (`<!-- design: Button -->`, or the language's comment form). Then the switch, which the hub performs and gates:

1. The agent calls `component_switch(name, code: <path>)` (or writes `code=` on the record through `artifact_update`; one tool, the same check).
2. **Override check.** The hub lists every `override` in use on instances of this component. The switch is refused while any remains: an override addresses inner nodes that will not exist. The agent resolves each by one of two patches: expose a prop (`titleColor: color`) in the code and rewrite those overrides as prop values on the instances (a hub patch by id, listed in the refusal), or detach that instance. No silent drop.
3. **Mount check.** The stage host compiles the file and mounts it once per instance with that instance's props and slots. Any compile or mount error returns `{file, line, column, message}` and the switch stays refused.
4. **Parity render.** Every artboard that uses the component is drawn twice — the design body and the code body — and pixel-diffed per instance (the probe kit's `pixelmatch` with the design's threshold). The result opens as a before/after artifact with the per-instance diff percentages; the verifier session (§5.7, never the builder) judges it, and the person can look. Acceptance is explicit: the agent passes the verifier's verdict to `component_switch(..., accept: true)`.
5. **Switch.** In one Yjs transaction: `code=` is set, the tree body is deleted, `ported="<framework>: <path> @ <commit>"` is recorded on the record. The instances are untouched: `of`, props, slots and ids are the same bytes. From this transaction the renderer takes the code path for them.

Nothing is ever rendered from both bodies at once except inside step 4. There is no way back to a design body; a change to the component after the switch is a change to the file, by the agent, on a pin.

A whole artboard ported as a screen becomes a code-backed component record of its own (`Screen.svelte` with the instances inside it); its instances on other artboards follow the same rule. Ports to a second target (SwiftUI, Flutter, React Native) add a second `ported=` entry; the canvas draws the one the project's stage host can run (the web one) and the others are proven on their platforms as today (simulator snapshots per the first spec's coverage note). The mapping table from the second spec (frame → HStack/VStack, Row/Column, flex View, flex div; slot → `@ViewBuilder`, widget parameter, `children`, Snippet; tokens → the target's token file) lives in the skill.

Traceability after the switch: `artifact_read(since: <the switch's cursor>)` lists the nodes changed since, which is the next coding task's work list; a pin on an instance names the file and, for a tap inside a rendered code instance, the exact `file:line:column` (§5).

## 5. Editing and pins

**The person, on the canvas** (own pan-and-zoom surface; no library: Excalidraw does not lay out flex DOM, Penpot is a whole application (own knowledge)):
- Select by tap, deeper by tap again, Esc up. Move (reorder inside flex with an insertion line; `x`/`y` in free frames; arrow-key nudge by one spacing step), resize (fixed; the inspector switches hug/fill), text in place, spacing/radius/colour through the token scale in the inspector (right panel; bottom sheet on phones), variant and other props as controls, swap instance, undo through `Y.UndoManager` scoped to the person's transactions (own knowledge of Yjs).
- **Design-backed component**: all of the above also inside the body (editing the master; every instance follows), and overrides on an instance's descendants.
- **Code-backed component**: props, slots, position and variant on the instance; a tap inside its render selects the inner element and the edit is a **pin**, because the inside is the file. Direct in-place edits of a code body's internals (text, spacing, colour) are not built; if the owner wants them later, they become edit-proposal pins `{file, line, column, property, from, to}` the agent applies — never an AST write-back by CawCo (the research report: no formatting-preserving printer for Svelte; Glide's regex path "too fragile").

**Pins, comments, ink** on any artifact, one payload: `{ node, component?, source? }` — `node` is the canvas node id (stable across edits; the "moved" tray is for deleted nodes); `component` is the record the node is inside; `source` is present when the tap landed inside a code-backed render: `{file, line, column}` from `__svelte_meta.loc` (+1, 0-based per the research report; refreshed from the DOM after every HMR update) or from `data-insp-path`. A comment therefore reads either "`a1.c2` (EventCard, roomy): tighter" or "`EventCard.svelte:42:6` inside `a1.c2`: heavier". Desktop taps on a `file:line` open the editor through Vite's `/__open-in-editor` on the host (own knowledge that Vite serves it; probe 2).

**The agent, through tools:**

| Tool | For a design |
|---|---|
| `artifact_create` | `kind: "design"`, `name`, `markup`. Answers id, route, markup with ids; refuses unknown components or tokens by name; parse errors with line. |
| `artifact_update` | `markup` merged by node id (nodes with the same id updated in place; selection, pins and unsent person edits survive — the tree's idiomorph), or `patch` by node id: `set`, `insert`, `move`, `delete`, `override`. Answers the markup after the change and the nodes the person changed since the last read, flagged. |
| `artifact_read` | Markup with ids, untokened nodes, pins, comments, picks, `changed` since a cursor, host `status`/`errors` for a code project; `png: true` renders the artboards (viewer render, or the hub's headless render; probe 5 decides the mechanism). |
| `design_library` | The project's component records: name, props, slots, body kind (`design`/`code`), `ported`. |
| `component_switch` | §4's handover: the override list, mount errors, the parity artifact, and the switch on `accept`. |
| `artifact_show`, `artifact_promote`, `comment_*` | Unchanged. Promote writes the design and its records to `design/`. |

Person edits reach the agent as today: batched after 3 s of quiet, at once during the turn; "Send N" for pins and picks. Host status and errors ride the same channel.

## 6. What this replaces and keeps

- **Replaced**: the OpenUI mockup library (`@cawco/core/mockups`, hub `mockups.ts`, `views/openui/mockup`, `system: "cawco"`, specimen templates). Its host, token loading, manifest and refuse-by-name are kept as the design renderer's; its primitives become base records; CawCo's own dashboard components become code-backed records in the cockpit repo's `design/components/` (declared signatures, no copies). Cutover, not alongside.
- **Kept**: OpenUI for live agent-made views with data (blocks, "Ask Caw for a view"); `page`, `canvas` (Excalidraw drawing), `preview` (a running app or folder, unchanged); the Yjs doc, pins, comments, picks, dials, ink, delivery, the panel.
- **Dropped**: "an agent reads an existing component and recreates it on the canvas" — in a code project the file is the component, and the only thing an agent writes about it is its signature line. The agent-written `.stage.svelte` from the first spec is gone too: the artboard is the stage, generated by the host from the tree.
- **Later, and what triggers it**: signature derivation from source (when manual declarations annoy); edit-proposal pins for code internals (if the owner asks); Script nodes (pen's live layers) when a design needs motion or data; Flutter through `flutter widget-preview start` and the simulator snapshot host for SwiftUI/Compose, when a project on those stacks wants its instances drawn rather than only ported.

## 7. The transcript cards, as it goes under this spec

`EventCard` and `StatusDot` are code-backed records (two signature lines). One design, one artboard, two instances with `density` as the pick, fixtures from the existing `cards.fixtures.ts`. The host mounts the real `EventCard.svelte` twice; the owner picks on the iPad and pins the roomy title; the agent edits `EventCard.svelte:42`; HMR re-draws both instances. Zero re-coded lines, no dev route, no server for the agent to keep alive.

## 8. What must be proven first

1. **Renderer parity across engines** (no-code path): three base records on an artboard, rendered in Chrome and the iPad web view; pixel diff < 0.5 %, differences only in text antialiasing. Fail → remove the engine-dependent property from the vocabulary.
2. **Code-backed mount under SvelteKit**: from `apps/dashboard`, the host serves the design page through the hub proxy; `EventCard.svelte` mounted twice with the instances' props and a fixture import; `$lib`, `app.css`, Tailwind resolve; an edit to the file re-draws both instances in < 1 s without reload; five inner elements' `__svelte_meta.loc` + 1 match the source; `/__open-in-editor` opens the file. Record whether `$app/state`'s `page` throws outside kit's root.
3. **Slots across the boundary**: a neutral `text` child in an instance's `footer` slot renders inside the Svelte component's snippet via `createRawSnippet`; the same for a React project's `children`. Fail → slot children for code bodies are limited to text and image until a per-framework path exists; said so, not hidden.
4. **Handover on one component**: a design-backed `Button` with two instances, one carrying an override; the switch refuses with the override listed; after the prop patch, the parity artifact shows two diffs under threshold; `accept` deletes the body and the instances render from code with the same ids.
5. **Headless render**: `artifact_read(png: true)` with no viewer attached, within 2 s per artboard; the probe records which mechanism it took.
6. **Lifecycle**: the host alive 30 min after the session's last turn; after `kill -9`, the next open renders within the warm budget; asleep and wake as specified.
7. **Agents write it**: five dashboard screens as markup from the generated prompt, by a Sonnet and an Opus session; ≤ 1 parse error per screen, each fixed from the error line on the next call.

## 9. What would change this

- If probe 3 fails for a framework, that framework's code bodies take only text and image slot children until its path is written; the contract is unchanged.
- If probe 2 shows SvelteKit's catch-all swallows `/__cawco/*` or `$app/*` cannot import outside kit's root: bring it to the owner; the options (an `appType: "custom"` server, or a design route inside the app's routes) touch the project.
- If probe 7 shows agents fight the markup, the tools accept the same tree as JSON too; the tree is unchanged.
- If the owner wants a code body's internals edited in place, edit-proposal pins are the mechanism; CawCo-side AST write-back stays out unless he authorises it, and then it is stylewright's method (parse offsets + magic-string splice) per framework.

I'm afraid Penpot does not have embed optios yet, but is something that we definitely want to do eventually. Thanks for raising the topic, this kind of comments help us to understand the level of interest and use cases ;)

 Jamby93 

Jun 27, 2025

Since this is the first github result if searching for "penpot iframe" on google, I'll share our solution: by enabling the un-documented (but still present, apparently "only for development" 

 penpot/common/src/app/common/flags.cljc 

| ;; enables the default cors configuration that allows all domains (currently this configuration is only used for development). |
| --- |

 ) flag "cors" (via PENPOT_FLAGS: enable-cors), we were able to embed iframes in our Confluence deploy. Without the flag enabled, the auth-token Cookie has SameSite Lax, which prevents it to be set if the top-level domain doesn't match the Penpot instance one (which is the case in any embedding, of course). With the flag enabled, SameSite is set to None, and the iframe works perfectly. This could of course raises some security concern (every origin is allowed to embed without any check), but since our Penpot and Confluence instances are segregated in our internal network, that is not a concern at all for us.

 SaadBazaz 

Much needed. It's pretty incomplete if there isn't the ability to add a Penpot frame (a direct one, instead of the entire file) in an Outline / Confluence / Notion doc.

Title: X-Frame-Options header - HTTP | MDN
URL: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/X-Frame-Options
Published: N/A
Author: N/A
Highlights:
Note: For more comprehensive options than offered by this header, see the `frame-ancestors` directive in a `Content-Security-Policy` header.

The HTTP `X-Frame-Options` response header can be used to indicate whether a browser should be allowed to render the document in a ` `, ` `, ` ` or ` `. Sites can use this to avoid clickjacking attacks and some cross-site leaks, by ensuring that their content is not embedded into other sites.

If this header is not sent, and the website has not implemented any other mechanisms to restrict embedding (such as the `frame-ancestors` CSP directive), then the browser will allow other sites to embed this document.
...
`DENY`
: The document cannot be loaded in any frame, regardless of origin (both same- and cross-origin embedding is blocked).
`SAMEORIGIN`
: The document can only be embedded if all ancestor frames have the same origin as the page itself.
`ALLOW-FROM origin` 
: This is an obsolete directive. Modern browsers that encounter response headers with this directive will ignore the header completely. The `Content-Security-Policy` HTTP header has a `frame-ancestors` directive which you should use instead.
...
Warning: Setting `X-Frame-Options` inside the ` ` element (e.g., ` `) has no effect. `X-Frame-Options` is only enforced via HTTP headers, as shown in the examples below.
...
To set `X-Frame-Options` to ... SAMEORIGIN` using Helmet add the following to your server configuration:
...
app.use(
  helmet({
    xFrameOptions: { action: "sameorigin" },
  }),
);

{"contentType":"text/html","creditCost":1,"markdown":"# 1.2  Install with Docker

[](https://penpot.app) [Try Penpot - It's free](https://penpot.app) 

Installing and maintaining a self-hosted Penpot instance requires some technical knowledge: Docker and Docker Compose, basic DNS management, and proxy configuration. If you're not comfortable with this stack, we encourage you to try more straight-forward installations with [Elestio](https://help.penpot.app/technical-guide/getting-started/elestio/) or use the SAAS at [https://design.penpot.app](https://design.penpot.app). 

# Install with Docker [#](#install-with-docker)

This section details everything you need to know to get Penpot up and running in production environments using Docker. For this, we provide a series of *Dockerfiles* and a *docker-compose* file that orchestrate all.

## Install Docker [#](#install-docker)

To host a Penpot instance with Docker, it's necessary to have `docker` and `docker compose` installed. Check the comprehensive [official documentation](https://docs.docker.com/) to install and maintain docker.

## Start Penpot [#](#start-penpot)

As a first step you will need to obtain the `docker-compose.yaml` file. You can download it [from the Penpot repository](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/penpot/penpot/main/docker/images/docker-compose.yaml).

```bash
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/penpot/penpot/main/docker/images/docker-compose.yaml
```

or

```bash
curl -o docker-compose.yaml https://raw.githubusercontent.com/penpot/penpot/main/docker/images/docker-compose.yaml
```

Then simply launch composer:

```bash
docker compose -p penpot -f docker-compose.yaml up -d
```

At the end it will start listening on [http://localhost:9001](http://localhost:9001)

If you don't change anything, by default this will use the latest image published in dockerhub. 

If you want to have more control over the version (which is recommended), you can use the PENPOT\_VERSION envvar in the common ways:

*   setting the value in the .env file
*   or passing the envvar in the command line

```bash
PENPOT_VERSION=2.4.3 docker compose -p penpot -f docker-compose.yaml up -d
```

## Stop Penpot [#](#stop-penpot)

If you want to stop running Penpot, just type

```bash
docker compose -p penpot -f docker-compose.yaml down
```

## Configure Penpot with Docker [#](#configure-penpot-with-docker)

The configuration is defined using flags and environment variables in the `docker-compose.yaml` file. The default downloaded file comes with the essential flags and variables already set, and other ones commented out with some explanations.

You can find all configuration options in the [Configuration](/technical-guide/configuration/) section.

## Using the CLI for administrative tasks [#](#using-the-cli-for-administrative-tasks)

Penpot provides a script (`manage.py`) with some administrative tasks to perform in the server.

**NOTE**: this script will only work with the `enable-prepl-server` flag set in the docker-compose.yaml file. For older versions of docker-compose.yaml file, this flag is set in the backend service.

For instance, if the registration is disabled, the only way to create a new user is with this script:

```bash
docker exec -ti penpot-penpot-backend-1 python3 manage.py create-profile
```

or

```bash
docker exec -ti penpot-penpot-backend-1 python3 manage.py create-profile --skip-tutorial --skip-walkthrough
```

**NOTE:** the exact container name depends on your docker version and platform. For example it could be `penpot-penpot-backend-1` or `penpot_penpot-backend-1`. You can check the correct name executing `docker ps`.

## Update Penpot [#](#update-penpot)

To get the latest version of Penpot in your local installation, you just need to execute:

```bash
docker compose -f docker-compose.yaml pull
```

This will fetch the latest images. When you do `docker compose up` again, the containers will be recreated with the latest version.

It is strongly recommended to update the Penpot version in small increments, rather than updating between two distant versions. 

#### Upgrade to 2.18 [#](#upgrade-to-2.18)

This version deploys a new service, **`penpot-admin-console`**, in the official `docker-compose.yaml` example. If you maintain your own compose file, you need to replicate the following changes manually:

**1\. Add the `enable-admin-console` flag**

**NOTE:** Enabling the Admin Console is not required in this version, but it will be in a future release. We recommend setting it up now to avoid a more complex upgrade later.

This step (the `enable-admin-console` flag) only applies to this version 2.18. In a future release, the Admin Console will be enabled by default and this flag will be removed. If you're upgrading directly to a version where the flag has already been removed, skip step 1 and go straight to steps 2–4, which remain required.

Wherever you set `PENPOT_FLAGS` (frontend and backend):

```diff
- PENPOT_FLAGS: disable-email-verification enable-smtp enable-prepl-server disable-secure-session-cookies enable-mcp+ PENPOT_FLAGS: disable-email-verification enable-smtp enable-prepl-server disable-secure-session-cookies enable-mcp enable-admin-console
```

**2\. Add the new `penpot-admin-console` service**

```yaml
  penpot-admin-console:
    image: "penpotapp/admin-console:2.18"
    restart: always

    depends_on:
      penpot-postgres:
        condition: service_healthy

    networks:
      - penpot

    environment:
      PENPOT_PUBLIC_URI: http://localhost:9001
      PENPOT_SECRET_KEY: change-this-insecure-key
      PENPOT_DATABASE_URI: postgresql://penpot-postgres/penpot
      PENPOT_DATABASE_USERNAME: penpot
      PENPOT_DATABASE_PASSWORD: penpot

      
      
      PENPOT_INTERNAL_URI: http://penpot-frontend:8080
```

> Use the same `PENPOT_PUBLIC_URI`, `PENPOT_SECRET_KEY`, and database credentials you already have configured for `penpot-backend`.

**3\. Update `penpot-frontend`**

*   Add `penpot-admin-console` to `depends_on`.
*   Add the following environment variable:

```diff
    environment:
      PENPOT_FLAGS: disable-email-verification enable-smtp enable-prepl-server disable-secure-session-cookies enable-mcp enable-admin-console
      PENPOT_HTTP_SERVER_MAX_BODY_SIZE: 367001600
      PENPOT_HTTP_SERVER_MAX_MULTIPART_BODY_SIZE: 367001600
      PENPOT_PUBLIC_URI: http://localhost:9001+
+     # Don't touch it; this uses an internal docker network to
+     # communicate with the admin-console.
+     PENPOT_ADMIN_CONSOLE_URI: http://penpot-admin-console:3000
```

**4\. Update `penpot-backend`**

Add the same variable:

```diff
    environment:
      PENPOT_FLAGS: disable-email-verification enable-smtp enable-prepl-server disable-secure-session-cookies enable-mcp enable-admin-console
      PENPOT_PUBLIC_URI: http://localhost:9001
      PENPOT_HTTP_SERVER_MAX_BODY_SIZE: 367001600
      PENPOT_HTTP_SERVER_MAX_MULTIPART_BODY_SIZE: 367001600
      PENPOT_SECRET_KEY: change-this-insecure-key+
+     # Don't touch it; this uses an internal docker network to
+     # communicate with the admin-console.
+     PENPOT_ADMIN_CONSOLE_URI: http://penpot-admin-console:3000
```

#### Upgrade from version 1.x to 2.0 [#](#upgrade-from-version-1.x-to-2.0)

The migration to version 2.0, due to the incorporation of the new v2 components, includes an additional process that runs automatically as soon as the application starts. If your on-premises Penpot instance contains a significant amount of data (such as hundreds of penpot files, especially those utilizing SVG components and assets extensively), this process may take a few minutes.

In some cases, such as when the script encounters an error, it may be convenient to run the process manually. To do this, you can disable the automatic migration process using the `disable-v2-migration` flag in `PENPOT_FLAGS` environment variable. You can then execute the migration process manually with the following command:

```bash
docker exec -ti <container-name-or-id> ./run.sh app.migrations.v2
```

**IMPORTANT:** this script should be executed on passing from 1.19.x to 2.0.x. Executing it on versions greater or equal to 2.1 of penpot will not work correctly. It is known that this script is removed since 2.4.3

## Backup Penpot [#](#backup-penpot)

Penpot uses [Docker volumes](https://docs.docker.com/storage/volumes) to store all persistent data. This allows you to delete and recreate containers whenever you want without losing information.

This also means you need to do regular backups of the contents of the volumes. You cannot directly copy the contents of the volume data folder. Docker provides you a [volume backup procedure](https://docs.docker.com/storage/volumes/#back-up-restore-or-migrate-data-volumes), that uses a temporary container to mount one or more volumes, and copy their data to an archive file stored outside of the container.

If you use Docker Desktop, [there is an extension](https://www.docker.com/blog/back-up-and-share-docker-volumes-with-this-extension/) that may ease the backup process.

If you use the default **docker compose** file, there are two volumes used: one for the Postgres database and another one for the assets uploaded by your users (images and svg clips). There may be more volumes if you enable other features, as explained in the file itself.

## Configure the proxy and HTTPS [#](#configure-the-proxy-and-https)

We strongly recommend to use Penpot under HTTPS/SSL, which will require specific server configurations for DNS and SSL certificates. Besides, your host configuration needs to make a proxy to [http://localhost:9001](http://localhost:9001).

If you plan to serve Penpot under different domain than \`localhost\` without HTTPS, you need to disable the \`secure\` flag on cookies, with the \`disable-secure-session-cookies\` flag. This is a configuration NOT recommended for production environments; as some browser APIs do not work properly under non-https environments, this unsecure configuration may limit the usage of Penpot; as an example, the clipboard does not work with HTTP. 

Below, you can see three examples with three different proxys:

### Example with NGINX [#](#example-with-nginx)

```bash
server {
  listen 80;
  server_name penpot.mycompany.com;
  return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl;
  server_name penpot.mycompany.com;

  
  
  client_max_body_size 367001600;

  
  access_log /path/to/penpot.access.log;
  error_log /path/to/penpot.error.log;

  
  ssl_certificate /path/to/fullchain;
  ssl_certificate_key /path/to/privkey;

  
  location /ws/notifications {
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection 'upgrade';
    proxy_pass http://localhost:9001/ws/notifications;
  }

  location /mcp/ws {
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection 'upgrade';
    proxy_pass http://localhost:9001/mcp/ws;
  }

  
  location / {
    proxy_set_header Host $http_host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Scheme $scheme;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_redirect off;
    proxy_pass http://localhost:9001/;
  }
}
```

For full documentation, go to the [official website](https://nginx.org/en/docs/index.html)

### Example with CADDY SERVER [#](#example-with-caddy-server)

```bash
penpot.mycompany.com {
        reverse_proxy :9001
        tls /path/to/fullchain.pem /path/to/privkey.pem
        log {
            output file /path/to/penpot.log
        }
}
```

For full documentation, go to the [official website](https://caddyserver.com/docs/)

### Example with TRAEFIK [#](#example-with-traefik)

In the [Penpot's docker-compose.yaml](https://github.com/penpot/penpot/blob/develop/docker/images/docker-compose.yaml) file, there is a simple example with Traefik. For full documentation, go to the [official website](https://doc.traefik.io/traefik/)
