## Decide
**Delete** a spec or proof when one of these holds:
- its feature is gone;
- another test proves all of it;
- it only re-proves what `bun run typecheck` / svelte-check / lint prove;
- it pins a one-off detail of a fix that later code has made impossible.

**Merge** two specs that set up the same fleet to prove neighbouring things into one, when that removes a duplicate setup run.

**Keep** everything else, and name the failure it guards.

Before deleting anything, read the commit that added it (the rule: find why something was added before removing it). Delete with its baselines and any helper only it used. Don't loosen a kept spec's limits, and don't add new specs.

Report one table:

| spec | asserts | added by | verdict | why |

Also report the totals (kept / deleted / merged), the deleted lines, and any spec you believe fails on main because the product is broken. For those, give the evidence. I decide on them; don't fix product code here."}}

7	WHAT CAWCO IS
8	CawCo (formal name Caw&Co) is a self-hosted control plane for AI coding agents. One operator runs Claude Code, OpenCode and pi sessions across their own machines. A hub on the LAN/tailnet (obelisk, http://192.168.3.100:3456) holds the fleet; each machine's agent reports to it. The dashboard shows every session live and lets the operator approve or deny permission requests, steer sessions and stop them. The apps make the phone, the tablet and the Mac the best places for the "needs you" part. The promise: an empty, connected board means nothing needs them, and a "needs you" is never missed.

10	MILESTONE 1
11	1. Connect: enter the hub URL once; it persists. Connection state is always visible: connected, reconnecting, unreachable.
12	2. Fleet board: every session with state, title, project, machine, harness and elapsed time, grouped the way the web board groups them.
13	3. Needs-you queue: the most prominent thing in the app. Approve and Deny work from it directly.
14	4. Session screen: native header (state; Stop; Steer with a message composer) and a native, live transcript.
15	5. Caw, the mascot, animated in the empty board, first run, loading and reconnecting states. Never inside rows, transcripts, errors or permission requests.
16	6. The same app on iPhone, iPad, iPhone Duo and Mac, light and dark, from the first commit.
17	Later, and not designed out: APNs push with Approve/Deny actions, Live Activities, widgets, App Intents, StoreKit, the Mac MenuBarExtra.

…[10305 chars clipped]…
d by `UIViewPropertyAnimator`. The zoom transition morphs between view controllers and carries a Catalyst caveat, so it is out.

153	Before the first screen:
154	- load `axiom:axiom-uikit` and read its `skills/adaptive-layout.md` and `skills/uikit-modernization.md`;

157	In short:
158	- Lay out by size class only, never by device model, idiom or orientation. The Duo's outer display is compact width; its inner display is regular; each half of Split View on the inner display is compact.
159	- Use `UISplitViewController` (board, then session), with bar items set on each view controller's `navigationItem` so the bars stay system-managed. Built with the 27.1 SDK, those bars lay out vertically along the side of the Duo. A custom `UIToolbar` or `UINavigationBar` never moves and gets no fold avoidance.
160	- Every bar item is a `UIBarButtonItem` with a title and an image, in this order:
161	  - back or close in `leadingItemGroups`;
162	  - the prominent action in `pinnedTrailingGroup`;
163	  - the rest after it, with `visibilityPriority` set so Approve and Deny overflow last, and extra actions in `additionalOverflowItems`.

The rail stacks these, in one vertical scroller:

Owner: "swipe between finished and working should be there", "the animation is a principle you should follow", "It should swipe just like in the models list and in the sidebar". The swipe works like this:
179	    - It follows the web's tab-swipe engine (`workspace/gesture.svelte.ts`): slop, then the direction locks, and mostly vertical is a scroll. The list region under the tab row drags off while its neighbour drags on, in lockstep with the finger, and the fluid-tabs indicator follows part-way.
180	    - It follows iOS practice (owner: "According to ios best practices"). The finger is tracked 1:1, the edges rubber-band like `UIScrollView`, and the release velocity is projected to pick the target, so a flick commits. The settle is an interruptible `UIViewPropertyAnimator` on a velocity-matched `UISpringTimingParameters` with no bounce, and a selection tick fires when the target tab changes (emil-design-eng, Gesture and Drag Interactions).
181	    - Whether swiped or tapped, the landing list's rows fly in staggered (owner: "Along with stagger fly in"), using the web's list-swap numbers: 18pt from the swipe's side plus a fade, 300ms, 40ms apart, capped at 9.
182	    - Past the first and last tab it moves against friction, not a hard stop. Extra touches are ignored once the drag starts.
183	    - It is built once and shared with the pane tabs.
184	    - The chrome never moves.
185	    - The system back swipe is arbitrated as below.
186	    - Reduce Motion gives a cross-fade.
187	  Paging the two whole panes moved the whole screen. The owner reported it on 2026-10-03: "the working/finished tabs don't animate properly (it transitoins the whole screen instead)". See `.context/parity/AUDIT.md` gap 2.
188	  - **The system's back swipe:** iOS 26's `interactiveContentPopGestureRecognizer` wins over the pager on the first tab, so arbitrate it in a gesture delegate. Never defer the system's bottom or left edge.
189	  - **Group swipe:** a two-touch `UIPanGestureRecognizer` on the container, arbitrated in its own delegate, with no `require(toFail:)` on the scroll pan because that delays one-finger scrolling. 190	  - **Splits:** the shell is `UISplitViewController`, with interactive column resizing and the inspector from iOS 26. No native or package nested split exists (PanelView, SplitKit and SplitPaneKit don't fit), so the pane tree mirroring the web's `workspace.svelte.ts` is our own code.

193	- State survives opening, closing and folding the Duo, rotation, and moving between Split View halves.
194	- Mac: the same UIKit app as a Mac Catalyst destination, optimized for Mac. 228	DESIGN
229	- Brand brief: `~/cawco-design-kit/prompt-1-design-system.md`. Palette: Ink #171715, Ivory #F4F0E6, Vermilion #E65D46, Butter #F2D36B; no indigo. Keep the two registers apart, use the status vocabulary, follow the copy voice. Brand art: `~/cawco-design-kit/01–05*.png`.

## What landed on the web and hub (commit 0f5a1f451, on main)
It was built from the owner's six pins on the task sheet.

**Hub.**
- `TaskView.result`: the newest finished attempt's full report (finish_item headline plus summary).
- `TaskAttempt.headline`: each attempt's one-line headline.
- `GET /api/projects/:id/tasks/:taskId/outputs/file?name=`: serves only the outputs the task declares; pictures as images, everything else as text.

Your client's `openapi.json` on main already has all three. Read `packages/hub/src/tasks.ts` and the `0f5a1f451` diff for their exact shape.

**Web sheet.** These files are your source of truth; read each one whole:
- `apps/dashboard/src/lib/cawco/tasks/TaskSheet.svelte`, `ResultView.svelte`, `ResultData.svelte`, `ResultTable.svelte`, `ResultCard.svelte`, `TaskAttempts.svelte`, `AttemptTranscript.svelte`, `result.ts`;
- `apps/dashboard/src/lib/cawco/project-tasks.ts`, for the API calls, Try again included.

What the web sheet does:
- **Header:** each fact named (Stage, Status, Waits on, Labels). Labels are badges that take no press; actions are buttons with a verb and a Solar duotone glyph.
- **Result section:** leads with the attempt's report (headline, then the summary as markdown). Each output is then drawn as what it is, never by its file name:
  - markdown as a document, front matter stripped, title not doubled;
  - HTML in a sandboxed frame;
  - `.json` as what it says: title, labelled fields, lists of records as tables;
  - CSV as a table;
  - pictures at their own size.
- **Attempts section:** "Each attempt is one session's try at this task." Tabs when there is more than one. Status in plain words ("Finished in 1 min", "Failed after 3 min"), how it ended, and Try again whenever no attempt is running.
- **Transcript:** the session's real transcript in a 30rem pane. Expand gives it its own full-height pane: beside the review on desk and tablet, over it on a phone.
- **Removed:** the old attempts list, the Retry block and the task-file path line.

One exception to parity: the web draws `.oui` outputs through the OpenUI mockup library (`MockupFrame`). The owner has just approved deleting that library (PRD D29, commit cdd94a2a4, `.design-foundations/plans/2026-10-16-live-components.md` §10), so don't build `.oui` rendering natively. Show a `.oui` output's text as code until that cutover removes it.

## The native file
`apps/apple/Packages/CawCoKit/Sources/CawCoScreens/Tasks/TaskSheetController.swift` currently draws attempts as rows. Rebuild the sheet to match the web. Use:
- UIKit only;
- `UICollectionView` with a compositional layout and a diffable data source for the sections;
- the app's existing `CawCoTranscript` views for both the transcript and the markdown (its TextKit 2 renderer);
- `WKWebView` with JavaScript off for HTML outputs;
- the app's `CawCoDesign` tokens and components for every colour, type, spacing and radius;
- `UISplitViewController`/sheet presentation as the app already does for this sheet.

Targets are iOS 18.0 and Mac Catalyst 18.0; anything newer goes behind `#available`.

Before writing code:
- Read `~/build` or main for the existing CawCoKit structure.
- Load these skills via the Skill tool: `write-swift`, `axiom:axiom-swift`, `axiom:axiom-concurrency`, `axiom:axiom-uikit`, `axiom:axiom-macos`, `axiom:axiom-networking` (the new route), `emil-design-eng`, `HIGAgentSkills`. Use any other installed skill that fits.
- List the skills you loaded in your report.

Builds and simulators go through `apps/apple/scripts/build-both.sh` and `mac-slot.sh`. The Xcode MCP (`xcode`, `xcrun mcpbridge`) drives the app; keep Xcode.app closed.

## Proof
Run each step once, on the final build; don't repeat a run unless the code changed.
1. Your item's check: `build-both.sh macos` launches. The hub adds the iOS compile check on its own.
2. The live check needs the hub on a build that serves the new fields. The fleet is on nightly 3353, which doesn't have them yet; I'm releasing the next nightly now, and the Mac's agent and the hub update themselves. Once `curl -s http://192.168.3.100:3456/api/agents` shows a build newer than 3353:

3. Commit and finish_item. If the nightly hasn't reached the hub by the time the build is done, finish with the build proof and say the live pairing is pending.

text: Launching skill: humanizer

Base directory for this skill: /home/bewinxed/.cawco/accounts/3c788add-0f48-4fe6-8b05-638c18bdc77a/claude/skills/humanizer

# Humanizer: Remove AI Writing Patterns

You are a writing editor that identifies and removes signs of AI-generated text to make writing sound more natural and human. This guide is based on Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" page, maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup.

## Your Task

When given text to humanize:

1. **Identify AI patterns** - Scan for the patterns listed below.
2. **Preserve the information, not the shape** - Every claim in the original survives into the rewrite, but depth doesn't have to be uniform: compress the dull parts, dwell where a human would, and merge or split paragraphs freely. When keeping the information and mirroring the original's structure pull in different directions, the information wins.
3. **Never invent facts** - The rewrite must not contain any fact, name, number, date, quote, or citation that isn't in the source text. Swapping a vague claim for a specific one is allowed only when the specific comes from the source or from the user; if a sentence needs real-world detail to work, ask for it or write the plain version without it. Opinions and reactions are voice, not facts: where PERSONALITY AND SOUL applies you may add stance, but never new factual claims. (In fiction, invented detail is the job. This rule governs everything else.)
4. **Match the voice** - Fit the intended tone (formal, casual, technical). Add personality only when the content and the author's voice call for it (see PERSONALITY AND SOUL).

How you're invoked changes what you deliver (see Invocation Modes). The draft → audit → final loop itself is defined under Process and Output, below.

## Voice Calibration

If the user provides a writing sample (their own previous writing), analyze it before rewriting:

1. Read the sample first. Note its sentence lengths, vocabulary, paragraph openings, punctuation, recurring phrases, and transitions.
2. Match those habits instead of merely deleting AI patterns. Do not upgrade casual words or regularize deliberate quirks.
3. Without a sample, use the default behavior below.

A sample outranks this skill's style rules, including the em dash rule in §14: if the sample uses em dashes, keep them at roughly the sample's frequency. Matching the author beats scrubbing the tell.

## PERSONALITY AND SOUL

Avoiding AI patterns is only half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious as slop. Good writing has a human behind it.

**Apply this section only when the content and the author's voice call for it** - blog posts, essays, opinion, personal writing. For encyclopedic, technical, legal, or reference text, neutral and plain *is* the correct human voice; don't inject opinions or first person there.

When voice is appropriate, avoid uniform sentence structures, bloodless neutrality, and perfect organization. Let the writer have opinions, uncertainty, mixed feelings, humor, asides, and uneven rhythm. Never add factual claims to create that personality.

## CONTENT PATTERNS

### 1. Undue Emphasis on Significance, Legacy, and Broader Trends

**Words to watch:** stands/serves as, is a testament/reminder, a vital/significant/crucial/pivotal/key role/moment, underscores/highlights its importance/significance, reflects broader, symbolizing its ongoing/enduring/lasting, contributing to the, setting the stage for, marking/shaping the, represents/marks a shift, key turning point, evolving landscape, focal point, indelible mark, deeply rooted
**Problem:** LLM writing puffs up importance by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects represent or contribute to a broader topic.
**Before:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was officially established in 1989, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics in Spain. This initiative was part of a broader movement across Spain to decentralize administrative functions and enhance regional governance.
**After:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was established in 1989, part of a wider decentralization of administrative functions in Spain.

### 2. Undue Emphasis on Notability and Media Coverage

**Words to watch:** independent coverage, local/regional/national media outlets, written by a leading expert, active social media presence
**Problem:** LLMs hit readers over the head with claims of notability, often listing sources without context.
**Before:**
> Her views have been cited in The New York Times, BBC, Financial Times, and The Hindu. She maintains an active social media presence with over 500,000 followers.
**After:**
> Her views have been cited in The New York Times and the BBC.

(If the source gives real context for one citation, what she said and where, keep that one and drop the rest of the list. Don't invent the context to make the trimmed version sound better.)

### 3. Superficial Analyses with -ing Endings

**Words to watch:** highlighting/underscoring/emphasizing..., ensuring..., reflecting/symbolizing..., contributing to..., cultivating/fostering..., encompassing..., showcasing...
**Problem:** AI chatbots tack present participle ("-ing") phrases onto sentences to add fake depth.
**Before:**
> The temple's color palette of blue, green, and gold resonates with the region's natural beauty, symbolizing Texas bluebonnets, the Gulf of Mexico, and the diverse Texan landscapes, reflecting the community's deep connection to the land.
**After:**
> The temple is painted blue, green, and gold, colors meant to evoke Texas bluebonnets and the Gulf of Mexico.

### 4. Promotional and Advertisement-like Language

**Words to watch:** boasts a, vibrant, rich (figurative), profound, enhancing its, showcasing, exemplifies, commitment to, natural beauty, nestled, in the heart of, groundbreaking (figurative), renowned, breathtaking, must-visit, stunning
**Problem:** LLMs have serious problems keeping a neutral tone, especially for "cultural heritage" topics.
**Before:**
> Nestled within the breathtaking region of Gonder in Ethiopia, Alamata Raya Kobo stands as a vibrant town with a rich cultural heritage and stunning natural beauty.
**After:**
> Alamata Raya Kobo is a town in the Gonder region of Ethiopia.

### 5. Vague Attributions and Weasel Words

**Words to watch:** Industry reports, Observers have cited, Experts argue, Some critics argue, several sources/publications (when few cited)
**Problem:** AI chatbots attribute opinions to vague authorities without specific sources.
**Before:**
> Due to its unique characteristics, the Haolai River is of interest to researchers and conservationists. Experts believe it plays a crucial role in the regional ecosystem.
**After:**
> Researchers and conservationists study the Haolai River for its unusual characteristics.

(If a real source exists, name it. Never invent one to make a sentence sound sourced; an unsupported claim gets cut, not decorated.)

### 6. Outline-like "Challenges and Future Prospects" Sections

**Words to watch:** Despite its... faces several challenges..., Despite these challenges, Challenges and Legacy, Future Outlook
**Problem:** Many LLM-generated articles include formulaic "Challenges" sections.
**Before:**
> Despite its industrial prosperity, Korattur faces challenges typical of urban areas, including traffic congestion and water scarcity. Despite these challenges, with its strategic location and ongoing initiatives, Korattur continues to thrive as an integral part of Chennai's growth.
**After:**
> Korattur has recurring traffic congestion and water shortages.

(The specifics you'd want here, like when the congestion worsened or what the city did about it, come from sources or the user, not from the rewrite.)

## LANGUAGE AND GRAMMAR PATTERNS

### 7. Overused "AI Vocabulary" Words

**High-frequency AI words:** Actually, additionally, align with, crucial, delve, emphasizing, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, highlight (verb), interplay, intricate/intricacies, key (adjective), landscape (abstract noun), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract noun), testament, underscore (verb), valuable, vibrant
**Problem:** These words appear far more frequently in post-2023 text. They often co-occur.
**Before:**
> Additionally, a distinctive feature of Somali cuisine is the incorporation of camel meat. An enduring testament to Italian colonial influence is the widespread adoption of pasta in the local culinary landscape, showcasing how these dishes have integrated into the traditional diet.
**After:**
> Somali cuisine also includes camel meat, which is considered a delicacy. Pasta dishes, introduced during Italian colonization, remain common, especially in the south.

### 8. Avoidance of "is"/"are" (Copula Avoidance)

**Words to watch:** serves as/stands as/marks/represents [a], boasts/features/offers [a]
**Problem:** LLMs substitute elaborate constructions for simple copulas.
**Before:**
> Gallery 825 serves as LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery features four separate spaces and boasts over 3,000 square feet.
**After:**
> Gallery 825 is LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery has four rooms totaling 3,000 square feet.

### 9. Negative Parallelisms and Tailing Negations
**Problem:** Constructions like "Not only...but..." or "It's not just about..., it's..." are overused. So are clipped tailing-negation fragments such as "no guessing" or "no wasted motion" tacked onto the end of a sentence instead of written as a real clause.
**Before:**
> It's not just about the beat riding under the vocals; it's part of the aggression and atmosphere. It's not merely a song, it's a statement.
**After:**
> The heavy beat adds to the aggressive tone.
**Before (tailing negation):**
> The options come from the selected item, no guessing.
**After:**
> The options come from the selected item without forcing the user to guess.

### 10. Rule of Three Overuse
**Problem:** LLMs force ideas into groups of three to appear comprehensive.
**Before:**
> The event features keynote sessions, panel discussions, and networking opportunities. Attendees can expect innovation, inspiration, and industry insights.
**After:**
> The event includes talks and panels. There's also time for informal networking between sessions.

### 11. Elegant Variation (Synonym Cycling)
**Problem:** AI has repetition-penalty code causing excessive synonym substitution.
**Before:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges. The main character must overcome obstacles. The central figure eventually triumphs. The hero returns home.
**After:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges but eventually triumphs and returns home.

### 12. False Ranges
**Problem:** LLMs use "from X to Y" constructions where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale.
**Before:**
> Our journey through the universe has taken us from the singularity of the Big Bang to the grand cosmic web, from the birth and death of stars to the enigmatic dance of dark matter.
**After:**
> The book covers the Big Bang, star formation, and current theories about dark matter.

### 13. Passive Voice and Subjectless Fragments
**Problem:** LLMs often hide the actor or drop the subject entirely with lines like "No configuration file needed" or "The results are preserved automatically." Rewrite these when active voice makes the sentence clearer and more direct.
**Before:**
> No configuration file needed. The results are preserved automatically.
**After:**
> You do not need a configuration file. The system preserves the results automatically.

## STYLE PATTERNS

### 14. Em Dashes (and En Dashes): Cut Them

**Rule:** The final rewrite contains no em dashes (—) or en dashes (–). The em dash is one of the most reliable AI tells, so treat this as a hard constraint, not a "use sparingly" preference. Replace each one, in rough order of preference: a period (start a new sentence), a comma (a tight aside), a colon (introducing an explanation), parentheses (a true aside), or restructure the sentence. Also catch spaced em dashes (` — `) and double hyphens (` -- `) used the same way.
**Before:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions—not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address—yet this mislabeling continues—even in official documents.
**After:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions, not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address, yet this mislabeling continues in official documents.
**Before:**
> The new policy — announced without warning — affects thousands of workers. The changes -- long overdue according to critics -- will take effect immediately.
**After:**
> The new policy, announced without warning, affects thousands of workers. The changes, long overdue according to critics, will take effect immediately.

Before returning the final rewrite, scan it for `—` and `–`. Any hit means the draft isn't done. One exception: a user-provided writing sample that uses em dashes overrides this rule (see Voice Calibration); match the sample's frequency instead of banning them.

### 15. Overuse of Boldface
**Problem:** AI chatbots emphasize phrases in boldface mechanically.
**Before:**
> It blends **OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)**, **KPIs (Key Performance Indicators)**, and visual strategy tools such as the **Business Model Canvas (BMC)** and **Balanced Scorecard (BSC)**.
**After:**
> It blends OKRs, KPIs, and visual strategy tools like the Business Model Canvas and Balanced Scorecard.

### 16. Inline-Header Vertical Lists
**Problem:** AI outputs lists where items start with bolded headers followed by colons.
**Before:**
> - **User Experience:** The user experience has been significantly improved with a new interface.
> - **Performance:** Performance has been enhanced through optimized algorithms.
> - **Security:** Security has been strengthened with end-to-end encryption.
**After:**
> The update improves the interface, speeds up load times through optimized algorithms, and adds end-to-end encryption.

### 17. Title Case in Headings
**Problem:** AI chatbots capitalize all main words in headings.
**Before:**
> ## Strategic Negotiations And Global Partnerships
**After:**
> ## Strategic negotiations and global partnerships

### 18. Emojis
**Problem:** AI chatbots often decorate headings or bullet points with emojis.
**Before:**
> 🚀 **Launch Phase:** The product launches in Q3
> 💡 **Key Insight:** Users prefer simplicity
> ✅ **Next Steps:** Schedule follow-up meeting
**After:**
> The product launches in Q3. User research showed a preference for simplicity. Next step: schedule a follow-up meeting.

### 19. Curly Quotation Marks
**Problem:** ChatGPT uses curly quotes (“...”) instead of straight quotes ("...").
**Before:**
> He said “the project is on track” but others disagreed.
**After:**
> He said "the project is on track" but others disagreed.

## COMMUNICATION PATTERNS

### 20. Collaborative Communication Artifacts

**Words to watch:** I hope this helps, Of course!, Certainly!, You're absolutely right!, Would you like..., Want me to...?, Want me to give examples?, Should I continue?, let me know, here is a...
**Problem:** Text meant as chatbot correspondence gets pasted as content.
**Before:**
> Here is an overview of the French Revolution. I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like me to expand on any section.
**After:**
> The French Revolution began in 1789 when financial crisis and food shortages led to widespread unrest.

### 21. Knowledge-Cutoff Disclaimers and Speculative Gap-Filling

**Words to watch:** as of [date], Up to my last training update, While specific details are limited/scarce..., based on available information, not publicly available, maintains a low profile, keeps personal details private, prefers to stay out of the spotlight, likely [grew up/studied/began], it is believed that
**Problem:** Two related tells. (a) Older models leave hard knowledge-cutoff disclaimers in the text. (b) When a model can't find a source, it writes a paragraph *about* not finding one and then invents plausible filler to cover the gap. For a private person the guess almost always lands on the same stock phrases ("maintains a low profile," "keeps personal details private"), none of it sourced. Say what isn't known, or cut the sentence; don't dress a guess up as fact.
**Before (cutoff disclaimer):**
> While specific details about the company's founding are not extensively documented in readily available sources, it appears to have been established sometime in the 1990s.
**After:**
> The company's founding date is not documented in the available sources. (Or cut the sentence. State a date only if a source provides one.)
**Before (speculative gap-fill):**
> Information about her early life is not publicly available, suggesting she maintains a low profile and keeps personal details private. She likely grew up in a middle-class household, which shaped her later interest in education reform.
**After:**
> Her early life is not documented in the available sources. (Or omit the section.)

### 22. Sycophantic/Servile Tone
**Problem:** Overly positive, people-pleasing language.
**Before:**
> Great question! You're absolutely right that this is a complex topic. That's an excellent point about the economic factors.
**After:**
> The economic factors you mentioned are relevant here.

## FILLER AND HEDGING

### 23. Filler Phrases

**Before → After:**
- "In order to achieve this goal" → "To achieve this"
- "Due to the fact that it was raining" → "Because it was raining"
- "At this point in time" → "Now"
- "In the event that you need help" → "If you need help"
- "The system has the ability to process" → "The system can process"
- "It is important to note that the data shows" → "The data shows"

### 24. Excessive Hedging
**Problem:** Over-qualifying statements.
**Before:**
> It could potentially possibly be argued that the policy might have some effect on outcomes.
**After:**
> The policy may affect outcomes.

### 25. Generic Positive Conclusions
**Problem:** Vague upbeat endings.
**Before:**
> The future looks bright for the company. Exciting times lie ahead as they continue their journey toward excellence. This represents a major step in the right direction.
**After:**
> (Cut the paragraph. End on the last concrete fact instead of a send-off. If the source states real plans, use those.)

### 26. Hyphenated Word Pair Overuse

**Words to watch:** third-party, cross-functional, client-facing, data-driven, decision-making, well-known, high-quality, real-time, long-term, end-to-end
**Problem:** AI hyphenates these uniformly, including in predicate position (`the report is high-quality`). Humans hyphenate inconsistently — typically only when the compound is attributive (`a high-quality report`) and often dropping the hyphen otherwise (`the report is high quality`). Keep attributive-position hyphens; drop them when the compound follows the noun.
**Before:**
> The cross-functional team delivered a high-quality, data-driven report. The team is cross-functional, the report is high-quality, and the methodology is data-driven.
**After:**
> The cross-functional team delivered a high-quality, data-driven report. The team is cross functional, the report is high quality, and the methodology is data driven.

### 27. Persuasive Authority Tropes

**Phrases to watch:** The real question is, at its core, in reality, what really matters, fundamentally, the deeper issue, the heart of the matter
**Problem:** LLMs use these phrases to pretend they are cutting through noise to some deeper truth, when the sentence that follows usually just restates an ordinary point with extra ceremony.
**Before:**
> The real question is whether teams can adapt. At its core, what really matters is organizational readiness.
**After:**
> The question is whether teams can adapt. That mostly depends on whether the organization is ready to change its habits.

### 28. Signposting and Announcements

**Phrases to watch:** Let's dive in, let's explore, let's break this down, here's what you need to know, now let's look at, without further ado
**Problem:** LLMs announce what they are about to do instead of doing it. This meta-commentary slows the writing down and gives it a tutorial-script feel.
**Before:**
> Let's dive into how caching works in Next.js. Here's what you need to know.
**After:**
> Next.js caches data at multiple layers, including request memoization, the data cache, and the router cache.

### 29. Fragmented Headers

**Signs to watch:** A heading followed by a one-line paragraph that simply restates the heading before the real content begins.
**Problem:** LLMs often add a generic sentence after a heading as a rhetorical warm-up. It usually adds nothing and makes the prose feel padded.
**Before:**
> ## Performance
>
> Speed matters.
>
> When users hit a slow page, they leave.
**After:**
> ## Performance
>
> When users hit a slow page, they leave.

### 30. Diff-Anchored Writing
**Problem:** Documentation or comments written as if narrating a change rather than describing the thing as it is. Unless the document is inherently version-scoped (changelogs, release notes, migration guides), it should read coherently without knowing what changed in the last commit.
**Before:**
> This function was added to replace the previous approach of iterating through all items, which caused O(n²) performance.
**After:**
> This function uses a hash map for O(1) lookups, avoiding the O(n²) cost of naive iteration.

### 31. Manufactured Punchlines and Staccato Drama
**Problem:** LLMs often make every sentence land like a quotable closer, then stack short declarative fragments to manufacture drama. A single short sentence for emphasis is fine; a run of them starts to sound engineered.
**Before:**
> Then AlphaEvolve arrived. It had no preference for symmetry. No aesthetic prior. No nostalgia for human taste. The old rules were gone.
**After:**
> AlphaEvolve changed the search because it did not favor symmetry or human-looking designs. That made some of the older assumptions less useful.

### 32. Aphorism Formulas

**Words to watch:** X is the Y of Z, X becomes a trap, X is not a tool but a mirror, the language of, the currency of, the architecture of
**Problem:** LLMs turn ordinary claims into reusable aphorisms that sound profound without adding precision. Replace the formula with the concrete claim it is gesturing at.
**Before:**
> Symmetry is the language of trust. Efficiency becomes a trap when teams forget the human layer.
**After:**
> Symmetric layouts often feel more predictable to users. Teams can over-optimize workflows and miss how people actually use them.

### 33. Conversational Rhetorical Openers

**Phrases to watch:** Honestly?, Look, Here's the thing, The thing is, Let's be honest, Real talk, when used as standalone hooks or fake-candid pauses before an ordinary point.
**Problem:** LLMs open with a fake-candid hook to manufacture intimacy before delivering a routine claim. The tell is the theatrical pause-and-reveal: a one-word question or aside, then the "real" answer. A person being honest usually just says the thing.
**Before:**
> Is it worth the price? Honestly? It depends on how often you'll use it.
**After:**
> Whether it's worth the price depends on how often you'll use it.

## DETECTION GUIDANCE

### What NOT to flag (false positives)

A clean human writer can hit several of the patterns above without any AI involvement. Before rewriting, sanity-check that you are not gutting legitimate prose. The following are *not* reliable indicators on their own:

- **Perfect grammar and consistent style.** Many writers are professionals or have been edited. Polish does not equal AI.
- **Mixed casual and formal registers.** This often signals a person in a technical field, a young writer, or someone with neurodivergent prose habits — not a chatbot.
- **"Bland" or "robotic" prose.** AI prose has *specific* tells. Generic dryness without those tells is just dry writing.
- **Formal or academic vocabulary.** AI overuses *specific* fancy words (see §7), not all fancy words. Don't flatten "ostensibly" or "constituent" just because they sound brainy.
- **Letter-style opening or closing on a comment.** Salutations and sign-offs predate ChatGPT by centuries.
- **Common transition words in isolation.** *Additionally*, *moreover*, *consequently* are AI-coded only when piled up. One *however* is not a tell.
- **Curly quotes alone.** macOS, Word, Google Docs, and most CMSes auto-curl by default. Curly quotes only count when stacked with other tells.
- **Em dashes alone.** Many editors and journalists use them often. Em dashes are evidence only when paired with formulaic sales-y rhythm.
- **One short emphatic sentence.** Humans use clipped sentences to land a point. Flag staccato drama only when several short fragments appear in a row and inflate the tone.
- **"Honestly" or "look" mid-sentence.** These are ordinary in casual writing. The tell is the standalone theatrical opener, not the word itself.
- **Unsourced claims.** Most of the web is unsourced. Lack of citations doesn't prove anything.
- **Correct, complex formatting.** Visual editors and templates produce clean output without any AI.
- **Secondhand text.** Do not rewrite watched phrases inside quotations, titles, proper names, or examples where the phrase is being discussed rather than used.

When in doubt, look for **clusters** of tells, not isolated ones. A single em dash means nothing; em dashes plus rule-of-three plus *vibrant tapestry* plus a "Conclusion" section is a confession.

### Signs of human writing (preserve these)

When you see these, lean toward leaving the prose alone — they are evidence of a real person writing, and over-editing will destroy what makes the piece sound human:

- **Specific, unusual, hard-to-fabricate detail.** A real address. A weird quote. The phrase "the lawyer who used to work upstairs from my dentist." LLMs round off specifics; humans hoard them.
- **Mixed feelings and unresolved tension.** "I think this is mostly good, but it bothers me, and I can't fully explain why." LLMs default to clean takes.
- **Dated, era-bound references.** Slang, memes, or in-jokes that map to a specific year and subculture. Models lag by a year or more.
- **First-person editorial choices the writer can defend.** If the writer can explain *why* they made a particular cut or used a particular word, that's a strong human signal.
- **Variety in sentence length.** Real writing alternates short and long. AI writing tends toward an even, mid-length cadence.
- **Genuine asides, parentheticals, or self-corrections.** "(I keep wanting to say 'almost' here, but it really was certain.)" Models rarely interrupt themselves like this.
- **Edits made before November 30, 2022.** ChatGPT's public launch. Anything older than that is, with very rare exceptions, not AI-written.

---

## Invocation Modes

**Pasted text (default).** The user gives text in the conversation. Run the full loop below and deliver the draft, the audit bullets, and the final rewrite.

**File mode.** The user points at a file. Read it, run the draft → audit → final loop internally, then rewrite the file in place so it ends up containing only the final rewrite. Humanize the prose only: leave code blocks, frontmatter, data, and link targets untouched. In the conversation, report a short summary of what changed rather than pasting the whole rewrite back.

**Embedded mode.** Another task or agent is using this skill as one step of a larger job (a PR description, a commit message, a doc). Run the loop internally and output only the final text. No draft, no audit bullets, no summary. The caller wants prose, not ceremony.

## Process and Output

1. Read the input carefully and identify every instance of the patterns above.
2. Write a **draft rewrite**. Check that it reads naturally aloud, varies sentence length, prefers specific details and simple constructions (is/are/has), and keeps the appropriate register.
3. Ask two questions: **"What makes the below so obviously AI generated?"** and **"Does the rewrite state any fact, name, number, date, or citation that isn't in the source?"** Answer briefly. A fabrication is a defect even when it sounds more human than the vague original.
4. Revise into a **final rewrite** that addresses them and contains no em or en dashes (see §14).

In pasted-text mode, deliver the draft, the brief "still-AI" bullets, the final rewrite, and (optionally) a short summary of changes. In file and embedded modes, run the same loop but deliver only what the mode calls for (see Invocation Modes).

## Reference

This skill is based on [Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Signs_of_AI_writing), maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup. The patterns documented there come from observations of thousands of instances of AI-generated text on Wikipedia.

Key insight from Wikipedia: "LLMs use statistical algorithms to guess what should come next. The result tends toward the most statistically likely result that applies to the widest variety of cases."

text:
312b43065 and 2a4808be8 landed with iOS compile errors: their items'
checks never compiled Swift, and no Linux check can. A project's Apple
build gate (projects.apple_gate, off by default; on for the cawco
repository by its migration) adds one check to an item that lands
somewhere when its diff against origin/<base> touches what the Swift
build reads: `bash apps/apple/scripts/build-both.sh ios --compile-only`
on an online apple-capable machine, at the item's last commit, through
the same path a brief's machine check runs (runChecks, the check
workspace there). With no Mac online the item does not land, and
finish_item says why in one sentence.

The paths are apps/apple/** and scripts/lib/heavy-run.sh (build-both.sh
sources it): the Swift sources and project, and every file generated into
the app (openapi.json, words, tokens, tool presentation). Core and hub
changes reach Swift only through those generated files, which
openapi:check and words:check keep in step; what those can't see is
whether Swift compiles against them.

The gate is set like Review before done: PATCH /api/projects/:id
`appleGate`, and Caw's project_settings `set_apple_gate`, always asked.
Probe: scripts/probe-kit/specs/apple-gate.ts (scratch fleet, stub Mac).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

/**
 * The Apple build gate: a project's setting (`projects.apple_gate`) that
 * keeps a work item from landing until the iOS app compiles at its last
 * commit. No Linux check compiles Swift, so a commit that breaks the app
 * passes every check a workspace there can run: 312b43065 changed a wire type
 * the TypeScript gates accepted, 2a4808be8 declared a Swift class twice, and
 * both landed with iOS compile errors.
 *
 * What it reads is the item's diff against its target. The paths that can
 * break the compile are the ones the Swift build reads:
 * - `apps/apple/**`: the Swift sources, the Xcode project, its resources and
 *   build scripts, and every file generated into the app from elsewhere: the
 *   OpenAPI document the Swift client is generated from (`bun run openapi`),

export const diffPaths = (stdout: string): string[] =>

Headline: The flaky across-update listener check came from the rig, not the product: a `podman exec -i` in the check's own pipe sometimes swallowed the process tree before grep read it. The check now reads the tree whole before judging it, and typecheck, lint and the rig's parse check pass.

Invariant: a release-proof check gives the same verdict on the same build every run. `workspace_across_update` failed about 1 run in 3 on the same build with "the listener N does not descend from the new sandbox's init M" (5856e71ec; 06ef5d1ac runs 2 and 6; ee79a01ea's "3971 … 3560" before that).

Cause, from the code and run 6's trace. The failing line was:
  ws_tree "$new_inner" | grep -qx "$(ws_listener_pid gen-new)" || { echo "ASSERTION FAILED: the listener … does not descend from the new sandbox's init …"; return 1; }
- The `$(…)` runs in the pipe's reading end, so ws_listener_pid's as_user (`podman exec -i …`, prove-stage2.sh as_user) inherits the pipe carrying ws_tree's output as its stdin.
- podman reads its stdin as soon as it starts. podman #24370 (https://github.com/containers/podman/issues/24370) says: "As soon as podman exec is launched it spawns a goroutine that reads data from stdin and sends it through a socket."
- When awk's tree reached the pipe before that exec finished, pgrep's podman swallowed it, grep saw no 4126, and the check failed. Run 6's trace shows pgrep's podman (log line 2248) starting beside awk (2251).
- A shell demo of the shape, `printf '4126\n' | grep -qx "$(cat > /dev/null; echo 4126)"`, gives no match.
- The old generation's check is the same pipe with a plain `$listener`, and it never failed.

The product placed the listener correctly every time:
- ws_same_sandbox passed just before the failure (`[[ 4003 == 4003 ]]`, line 2240), so the sandbox never started again.
- The command before it ran in 4003's own pid namespace (`pid:[4026538091]` on both sides).
- The kernel's find_new_reaper reparents every orphan inside its own namespace.
- Nothing enters the sandbox's pid namespace from outside: preview-bridge.ts:70 joins only --user and --net.
- ee79a01ea's report had the listener "in generation da40b3e7's cgroup".

Fix, in scripts/binary/prove-stage2.sh (37d504f3c, on top of 63a9d80a0):
- `ws_descends PID INIT` reads the tree into a variable with its own exit status. An unreadable process table fails as "the joined machine's process table could not be read (exit N)".
- It judges with `grep -qx "$1" <<< "$tree"`, so no pipe is shared with a podman exec.
- Only when the listener is outside the tree does it print the tree and the listener's parents (`ws_ancestry`: pid, ppid, start, pid ns, cgroup, command line).
- Both listener checks (old and new generation) use it. Check names are unchanged, the new helpers are in `export -f`, and there are no sleeps or retries.

The redesign is built at ws/a4e27882 (typecheck and lint:changed pass). It fails the two-pane-perf spec. One decision is needed from you or the owner.

Built, driven by a profile of each switch's longest task sampled alone (one run, then the spec once):
- `lifting`'s forced flush: 27–34ms per switch, from the composer tray crossfade. It now keeps the fade Svelte starts; no animation listing.
- Pane `inert` is set only when drawn and not active (content-visibility: hidden already keeps put-away panes out of tab order, per MDN).
- Tab track: scroll offset and edge room as last laid out; the fade is found a frame on.
- `reflow()` ignores changes that only swap Svelte's anchors, so the composer's offer slot no longer measures on a hand-off.

The finish_item spec run:
- stream: PASS, 1.10x.
- type: PASS, 0.97x; slowest key 56ms.
- cold: PASS, 108 vs 91ms.
- point: 64 (one pane) / 83 (two panes) ms CPU. FAIL.
- focus: 62 / 66 ms CPU. FAIL.

What it shows: removing the forced reads moved the style and layout to the next reader in the frame (the reflow anchor's scrollTop, the glass card's rect). The switch's actual work stays the same:
- one pane: ~31ms of style over 500–600 elements plus 13–15ms of layout;
- two panes: ~41–47ms of style over ~2,250 elements plus 13ms of layout.
That matches the incoming pane's whole subtree being restyled as an inherited property flips on its root at the click (`visibility` from `.pane-settling`). In two panes each pane holds 1,000–1,700 elements.

Getting under 25ms means no inherited change on that pane at the click. The only ways to keep a warm pane hidden without one are opacity:0 / z-index under the shown pane. During the warm window (hover or focus plus 1.5s), the warm pane's controls would then be reachable by Tab and exposed to screen readers. Options:
- (a) Accept that a11y trade-off for the warm window.
- (b) Cut what a pane mounts (virtua overscan and TAIL_MOUNTED), so the flip restyles fewer elements. This is uncertain to reach 25ms with long transcripts.
- (c) Land at the measured ~60–80ms with the spec thresholds set to it.
Which?

Headline: Both iOS crashes are fixed in one commit: transcript updates no longer reconfigure rows they leave out, and the transcript's frame stops running while the app is in the background. A simulator probe crashed the shipped code path both ways before the fix.

Commit 98bc3f54d (rebased on main at c2d7695b3).

1. OPEN/RELAUNCH CRASH. The phone's .ips shows NSInternalInconsistencyException from -[__UIDiffableDataSourceSnapshot _validateReloadUpdateThrowingIfNeeded:] under reconfigureItems, in TranscriptView.commit(fresh:), called from the display link. commit() collected the rows to reconfigure from what the list held before, but applied a snapshot of `next`. The first screen is a window over the rows, and that window moves, empties while a restored place is read back to, or flips to the tail. So a held row redrawn in the same frame could be reconfigured in a snapshot that no longer contained it. Fix: `changed.removeAll { !next.holds($0) }`, applied once where `next` is built, before both redrawInPlace and the snapshot.

2. APPROVAL CRASH (5e7ba196f35b55c6): a watchdog kill, 8BADF00D "scene-update watchdog transgression", 10 s of wall time at 17% CPU on the way to the background. The main thread was in the frame's first-screen layout. While the app goes to the background the system lays it out itself to take its snapshots, and the frame kept laying out and committing rows under it on every display frame. Fix: in the background the link stays paused and wake() can't unpause it. A scene restored into the background starts paused. On coming forward the pane wakes once and draws what changed.

38	## 2. Running it: the stage
39	
40	**Recommendation.** One **stage** per workspace, owned by the daemon's supervisor, running the project's own toolchain in the project's own runtime inside the workspace sandbox, with one CawCo plugin added at start and nothing installed into the project.
41	
42	**Start.** The daemon writes `.cawco/stage/host.mjs` (CawCo's embedded script, git-excluded) and spawns it with the runtime the lockfile implies: `bun` if `bun.lock`/`bun.lockb`, else `node`. The host runs in the project's runtime and imports the project's own `vite`/`astro`/`nuxt`/`next` from the workspace's `node_modules`; CawCo's binary only supervises. **Own call**, and it makes spike (5)'s question (can the compiled Bun binary `import()` a runtime-written `.mjs`?) moot: the binary never imports the toolchain. If the spike shows the binary can, the design stays as written: the project's Vite version must not be coupled to CawCo's process.
43	
44	**Per toolchain, how the plugin gets in without editing the user's config:**
45	
46	| Toolchain | How the host starts it | Source |

54	**What the plugin serves** (kept from the merged spec §3, trimmed): `GET /__cawco/sheet?file=<repo-relative .stories.ts>` → an HTML shell built from the project's own `index.html`/`app.html` (so global CSS, fonts and tokens load), importing a virtual module `cawco:sheet?file=…` that imports the story file, reads `default.component`, `default.args`, `default.decorators`, and each named export's `args`/`render`/`decorators`, and mounts each story into its own frame with the framework's mount function. Mount adapters are the only per-framework code: Svelte `mount(Component, { target, props })`, Vue `createApp(Component, props).mount(target)`, React `createRoot(target).render(createElement(Component, props))`, Solid `render`, Preact `render`. HMR: the sheet module accepts updates (`import.meta.hot.accept`) and re-mounts affected frames with the same args; editing `EventCard.svelte` redraws every instance in place. **Spike (2)** measures HMR latency and HMR through the hub's proxy. If HMR does not pass the proxy: the plugin sets `server.hmr.path` and `clientPort` to the preview's own origin (the hub gives every preview "an origin of its own, never the dashboard's", `packages/hub/src/preview.ts`), so no path prefix is involved.
55	
56	**Lifecycle** (one supervisor rule set, no agent in the loop): start on the first `artifact_create(kind: "sheet")` or first open; `ready` within 60 s or `error`; health `GET /__cawco/health` every 15 s; restart ×3 with backoff then `error`; asleep after 30 min with no viewer and no agent read; wake on open; stop when the workspace is archived. Panel states: Starting ("Starting vite in `apps/dashboard`…"), Compiling, Error, Live, Asleep ("Waking…"). The stage listens on a port inside the workspace and is shown through the existing `port:<port>@<workspace>` preview source (`packages/agent/src/preview-bridge.ts`), so desktop and the iPad's web view get the same overlay-injected page.
57	
58	**Errors to the agent.** The plugin turns Vite's error payload (`message`, `loc: { file, line, column }`, `frame`) into `status.errors` on the artifact; the hub delivers it on the same batched channel as pins (3 s quiet, at once during a turn). The overlay draws CawCo's error card over the dimmed last render; Vite's own overlay is off (`server.hmr.overlay: false`). **Spike (4)** proves compile errors are captured as JSON and cleared on the next good compile. If Vite's payload lacks `loc` for a framework, the error carries `file` from the failing module id and no line.
59	
60	## 3. The canvas: instances and variants side by side
61	
62	**Recommendation.** A sheet renders as one page: a horizontal row (wrapping) of frames, one frame per story, each labelled with the story's name, each hugging its content; a story's width is `parameters.viewport` when set (Storybook's own key), otherwise content width. This is what pen.dev and Paper show: component states laid out as separate frames on an artboard (Paper's documented workflow: "a `Component States` artboard detailing every default / hover / active state", https://github.com/gergelyszerovay/skills/blob/main/paper-to-react-workflow.md). Viewport presets (phone, tablet, desktop), light/dark and reduced-motion toggles are the panel's chrome (D18's list) and apply to the whole sheet: the stage page reads them from the URL and sets `color-scheme`, width and `prefers-reduced-motion` emulation via a wrapper class.
63	
64	**On top of it, unchanged:** the overlay the hub already injects into every preview (`injectOverlay`, `packages/hub/src/preview.ts`). Picks (D19): the sheet is a choice, its stories the options; a pick stores `{ choice: <story file>, option: <export name> }` in the hub as today. Pins and comments (D20, tsk-3) anchor to elements by selector as today, plus `source` (§4). Pencil ink (D27) anchors to the deepest element under the stroke as today; its radial menu's Comment and Annotate produce pins carrying `source`. Nothing in D24–D27 changes.
65	
66	**The Excalidraw canvas (D24) is not the venue.** It does not lay out live DOM; a sheet is a `preview`-class artifact. A session that wants to sketch over a sheet draws with ink (D27), or the agent puts a PNG of the sheet (`artifact_read(png: true)`) onto a canvas. Kept from the merged spec: no pan-and-zoom surface of CawCo's own.

68	## 4. Source mapping per framework, and what a pin carries
69	
70	**Recommendation.**
71	
72	| Framework | Element → source | Call site (which instance) | Source |
73	|---|---|---|---|
74	| Svelte 5 | `el.__svelte_meta.loc = { file, line, column }`, 0-based; dev compile only | `__svelte_meta.parent` chain up to the story mount | `svelte/src/internal/client/dev/elements.js` and vite-plugin-svelte's inspector (prior-art report §4: `file_loc = ${file}:${line + 1}:${column + 1}`, commit `4158aa2` walks `parent` to "where a component is used"). **Spike (3)** checks accuracy and the chain. If `loc` is off for some elements: fall back to the plugin's stamp (next row) for Svelte too, one mechanism for all. |
75	| React 18/19, Preact, Solid, Qwik, Vue 3, Astro | `data-insp-path="<file>:<line>:<column>:<tag>"` stamped by code-inspector's transforms (MIT), vendored into the stage plugin | component roots read `props['data-insp-path']`, so a root element carries the call site | prior-art report §6; React 19 "Remove `__self` and `__source` location from elements … all the places using it like the `_debugSource` on Fiber" (https://github.com/facebook/react/pull/28265) broke every fiber-reading tool (list in that thread: react-dev-inspector, locatorjs, code-inspector, click-to-component…); compile-time stamping "is the only approach that works reliably across React 18, React 19, and all modern bundlers" (https://github.com/ivanstnsk/xray). Vue's own inspector "records source locations from Vue's compiled render output with Vite source maps, and uses dev-only `data-v-inspector` DOM markers as a fallback" (https://github.com/webfansplz/vite-plugin-vue-inspector); the stamp is the simpler, uniform one. |
76	| Angular | none | none | refused in §2 |

79

81	{
82	  "artifact": "<id>",
83	  "sheet": { "file": "src/lib/cawco/transcript/EventCard.stories.ts", "story": "Roomy" },
84	  "anchor": { "selector": "…", "box": { "x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 0, "h": 0 } },
85	  "source": { "file": "src/lib/cawco/transcript/EventCard.svelte", "line": 42, "column": 6 },
86	  "chain": [
87	    { "component": "EventCard", "file": "…/EventCard.svelte", "line": 1, "column": 0 },
88	    { "component": "Roomy", "file": "…/EventCard.stories.ts", "line": 18, "column": 2 }
89	  ],

91	}

93	
94	`source` is the tapped element's own tag (1-based line and column, converted at read time); `chain` is the ancestors from the element's component up to the story, so an agent can tell "inside EventCard" from "the story's args". A comment therefore reads "`EventCard.svelte:42:6` inside story Roomy: heavier".

Headline: Port previews now refuse the dev-server routes that open an editor or debugger on the machine, and drop Vue DevTools' unauthenticated file-read RPC on the HMR socket. Against a real Vite dev server, `/__open-in-editor?file=/etc/hostname` launched the editor before the change and answers CawCo's 403 after; the app and its HMR still work through the same preview.

## Routes, with sources
Read from each package's published source (npm tarballs) and from Vite's repo on GitHub.
- **Vite `/__open-in-editor`**: https://github.com/vitejs/vite/blob/main/packages/vite/src/node/server/index.ts says `middlewares.use('/__open-in-editor', launchEditorMiddleware())`. It runs before the transform and static middlewares; connect matches the mount case-insensitively and lets `/__open-in-editor.x` through.
- **launch-editor-middleware**: it has no path of its own (https://github.com/yyx990803/launch-editor/blob/master/packages/launch-editor-middleware/index.js resolves `?file=` and calls `launch(resolved, …)`). Its README's default mount is `app.use('/__open-in-editor', launchMiddleware())`.
- **webpack-dev-server 6.0.0** (lib/Server.js): `path: "/webpack-dev-server/open-editor"`, then `launchEditor(fileName)`. It does check `#isSameOriginRequest`, but that check passes behind CawCo (see below).
- **CRA / react-dev-utils 12.0.1**: launchEditorEndpoint.js is `module.exports = '/__open-stack-frame-in-editor'`, and errorOverlayMiddleware.js calls `launchEditor(req.query.fileName, …)`.
- **Next.js 16.4.2**: dist/server/dev/middleware-turbopack.js has `pathname === '/__nextjs_launch-editor'` → `openFileInEditor(…)`. Also attach-nodejs-debugger-middleware.js: `'/__nextjs_attach-nodejs-inspector'` → `_inspector.open(debugPort)`. That opens a code-execution endpoint on the server, and its only use (a DevTools link to the server's loopback) can't work through a preview, so it is refused too.
- **Nuxt DevTools 3.4.3**: its server RPC rides Vite's HMR socket as custom event `nuxt:devtools:rpc`. Every function that writes files, runs commands or takes a path calls `ensureDevAuthToken(token)` first. The token lives in `~/.nuxt/devtools/dev-auth-token.txt` and is shown only on the server's terminal ("A browser is requesting permissions of writing files and running commands"). The check isn't origin-based, so it still holds behind CawCo, and this channel is left alone.
- **But Nuxt also adds vite-plugin-vue-devtools (8.x)**, and that plugin's RPC has no token: `getTextAssetContent(filepath)` returns `(await fsp.readFile(filepath,'utf-8')).slice(0, limit)` for any path, and `getImageMeta(filepath)` likewise. It travels as custom event `__devtools-kit-vite-messaging-event-key__` (@vue/devtools-kit). This is the one HMR channel refused.
- **SvelteKit 3.1.0**: no editor route of its own. The Svelte inspector (vite-plugin-svelte 7.3.1, Inspector.svelte) does `fetch(`${base}/__open-in-editor?file=…`)`, which is Vite's route.
- **Astro 7.4.0** dev toolbar and overlay (xray.js, audit-ui.js, overlay.js): `fetch("/__open-in-editor?file=" + …)`, also Vite's route.
- **@vitejs/devtools 0.8.0**: its `vite:core:open-in-editor` RPC sits behind devframe's interactive one-time-code auth on a sidecar WebSocket port, not the app's port. Left alone.
- **Judged out:** Next's `/__nextjs_restart_dev` restarts the dev server and can clear its build cache. It doesn't open a file or run a new program, and Next's own dev indicator uses it.

## Where the rule lives, and why
In the agent's preview listener (`packages/agent/src/preview.ts`), not the shared preview-proxy code:
- **Every port preview passes through it.** The hub only relays port previews to the machine's listener (`relay` in hub/preview.ts). Folder and page previews never reach a dev server.
- **It binds `0.0.0.0`.** Anyone on the LAN or tailnet can reach it without going through the hub, so a rule at the hub alone would miss those requests.
- **It is the hop that defeats the dev servers' own checks.** It rewrites Host, Origin and Referer to `localhost:<port>` (preview.ts, the port branch), so webpack-dev-server's same-origin check and Vite's HMR origin check pass for any viewer. The refusal sits just before that rewrite.

Putting it in the shared code too would run it twice for nothing.

Two parts, one place:
- **Paths:** `machineRoute(url.pathname)` matches the route segments anywhere in the decoded, lower-cased path (so a `base`/`basePath` prefix is covered), and a last segment followed by `.` (connect's matching). It answers a plain-text 403: "CawCo refused /__open-in-editor: it would open a file or a program on the machine serving this preview, and a preview only shows its app. Open the file from that machine instead." It also writes one journal line through `previewFailed`.
- **HMR frames:** `listenerSocket` wraps the core `previewWebSocket`. On `vite-hmr` sockets only (Vite's ws.ts upgrades nothing else), it drops a frame whose JSON (text or bytes; Vite reads `JSON.parse(String(raw))`) is `{type:"custom", event:"__devtools-kit-vite-messaging-event-key__"}`. Every other frame goes on.

No broad path rules: `/@vite/*`, `/@fs/` and the app's own routes are untouched, and Vite still enforces its own `fs.allow`.

3	description: "Owner rules for UI, design, motion, copy, Caw art and site briefs. Read before writing any of them; owner-rules.md points here."

8	---
9	
10	## The design workflow, in order, and nothing else
11	1. I settle the product model and the exact content of every row and screen myself, from the live page, the owner's notes and "Text is earned". The live page is measured from its DOM (computed border, padding, row height, background), never taken from a reviewer's or my own description (2026-10-09: I specced "one inset card" while the live list was flat hairline rows). A complaint is answered by re-deriving from the live page, never by patching the last design one sentence at a time.
12	2. A Fable `advisor` gets the four things only (fleet CLAUDE.md): exact files, current screenshots, the requirement (my content file plus his notes verbatim), the ask (fit plus wireframe). It returns the fit and the wireframe, never content decisions or a build spec. A design brief gives the requirement and the screens it must fit, never the shape: no pre-listed rows, states or buttons (the Mac readiness brief listed rows and got "a bunch of controls").
13	3. An Opus leaf builds that wireframe from real components with the exact spec I write. Mockups never go to Sonnet.
14	4. A Sonnet review (`clearshot` + `interface-craft` Design Critique) of the captures against DESIGN.md and the approved design, dispatched by me before he or a TestFlight sees the screen. A designer's added content (dials, meta lines, status words) is checked against "Text is earned" there.
15	5. He picks; 6. I write the build spec.
16	Owner: "are you letting sonnet design the ui or yourself? … mocks go on an opus leaf with exactly what it needs to do", "that isn't the agreed-upon ui design workflow :/", "today's mockups and designs have been really suboptimal. It seems like they are not taking into account the layout or our design".
17	
18	**Skills.** Every UI leaf and advisor loads `interface-craft` and `emil-design-eng`; designers also `axiom:axiom-design`. Every brief that designs or writes motion (web or Apple, advisor or build) loads `emil-design-eng` and `transitions-dev` (exact name). Owner: "all ui work should use /interface-craft ux ui principles and /emil-design-eng", "Are you passing emil kowalski animation skill too", "use /transitions-dev for the animation leaf".
19	
20	**Previews.** A design preview is an artifact page of only the changed elements: a small standalone build of the real components with fixture data, one control per state or action, opened with `artifact_create(kind: "page", dir)`; never the whole app on a dev server with a scratch fleet (owner: "why do you waste time spinning up a whole preview etc with the whole app instead of having an artifact where u show the changed elements with a simple state machine"). Only when a design has real alternatives; a simple change proven by its probe lands with no preview (owner: "ur wasting time building a preview for somethign that is so very simple"). Subtle visual choices go to him as real captures, enlarged, press-and-hold for original, or as annotated images or short animations of exactly what differs, never numbers or a live page to explore (owner: "These all literally look the same, use screncaps", "u keep using live previews in your mockups instead of images or animations"). Every edit to a page he is viewing is followed by showing it again (owner: "If u modify the preview u should launch it again mate"). A copy or requirement change to a designed screen gets a layout pass with a copy budget before the build (the paywall became a "wall of text").
21	
22	**Inline detail is discussed out loud before any rewrite**: an interface-craft critique and a proposed text wireframe first, then his go (owner: "don't rewrite the inline without discussing with me first OUT LOUD"; "this is the 5th time").
23	
24	## Principles every UI brief states
25	- **Stay in context** (DESIGN.md's Stay In Context Rule, c9719da0): brief the principle, never a pattern's parts. Four questions: where is their attention (the flow happens there; the thing acted on becomes its result); what do they need to decide (real consequences, before they commit); what is true now (the system's word, progress on what changes); what if it fails (same place, same state, told what happened, able to go on). A light action changes in place; a heavy one names what it reaches. `ForgetProjectDialog.svelte` is one worked answer, reused only where a flow asks the same questions. Reviews grade by the four questions, never by whether a flow has a tray, ring or two-step arming. Owner: "This fluid ux is the bar for any part of this project. Keeps the user in context", "now you'll end up copying the pattern instead of the first principle philosophy".
26	- **Onboarding and setup** continue the flow they belong to, never a panel of controls: automatic checks tick as live rows, it stops at the first thing that needs the person and shows only that step (Caw, one line, one button), advances itself, asks optional things only when a session needs them. Models: Connect a machine's step list, `home/Home.svelte`, `home/Caw.svelte`, the paywall's S1–S4. Owner: "a bunch of controls thrown on a page is NOT acceptable", "all of this should happen when adding a machine".
27	- **No useless UI and no repeated obvious info**: no ids; the machine once as a header, not per row; no "working" label under a Working tab; no "nothing needs you" filler; no labels restating icons, sections or neighbours (owner: "no useless ui elements and no repeating obvious info in the ui").
28	- **Text is earned**: no subtitles, eyebrows or meta lines restating the screen; a list row is its title; a second line only for a fact the person must act on, written as that fact ("Not signed in on gauntlet"); trailing controls in one fixed column; usage dials only where approved (rail, phone strip, popover, Usage page). Owner: "too much text and \"eyebrow\" text, meaningless".
29	- **Spend is not UI content**: cost, caps and meters never appear in a view, row or inline detail; a cap is a setting in its Edit; a run the cap stopped says so in its run line (owner: "nobody puts spend in the ui first thing", "this should be a footnote, not the main design").
30	- **Error states** follow standard recovery UX: clear error, why, recovery actions; never offer "fail vs hold" as a choice (owner: "agreed-upon ux patterns for error recovery").
31	- **Motion comes from DESIGN.md's motion language and tokens**, not references or a designer's invention (owner: "u should adopt the motion language from our own design guidelines").
32	- **Copy** never says "tap", "poke" or the like about reaching the person (owner: "'tap you' is harassment").
33	
34	## House patterns a brief must name
35	- **Motion helpers**: `morph()` (`$lib/cawco/motion/`) for any box whose content changes size; `NsPopoverGroup` for one surface moving between triggers; `reflow()` + `data-flip` for lists; `unfold` for rows that open. A leaf not told builds its own (owner, on the tray hover card: "WHICH IS THE PATTERN USED ACROSS THE APP SO WHY WASN'T IT DONE THIS WAY").
36	- **Tab switches** reuse the New session modal's harness switch exactly (ModelSection.svelte: thumb slide, `.leaving` rows out with `leaveAnim`, gen-keyed rows staggering in, container height following) as one shared primitive with identical timings; a copy that looks wrong is unfaithful, fix the copy. What both tabs share (machine headers) stays put; only differing rows stagger; group heights follow via `morph()`. The header is `$lib/components/ui/fluid-tabs`: `variant="folder"` where tabs open a page (PaneTabs, sidebar Working/Finished), segmented inside a block; never hand-rolled. Owner: "the tab switch pattern is in the new session modal", "the machines are the same in working/finished … can swap out the sessions only", "use the same tab style as the session tabs".
37	- **Nesting is lines, app-wide** (`.kit-nest`): neutral ink ≥3:1 on the surface in both themes; no chevron where lines show nesting; lines draw and retract on expand/collapse; no highlight pill covers a line; sidebar tab rows have no background; no stacks, recursive nesting, no lines at a project's first level. Headline: Host checks and delegate inputs are built: a check its parent marks host runs outside every sandbox on a fresh checkout of the item's commit, and delegate and handoff copy named files into the delegate's $TMPDIR/inputs/. Typecheck, lint and the tool budgets pass on the rebased tree; the host-checks probe still needs its one run on the host.

## What was built

**1. `checks[].host: true`** can be declared on delegate and set_item_checks (zod schema and the hub's body schema), and in task files as `host: <command>` (dispatch.ts `checksOf`).

The mechanism this reuses is in work-items.ts `runChecks`. A check with `machine` ran in a check workspace that `elsewhere()` prepared: `CONTROL_WORKSPACE_BUNDLE`, then `CONTROL_WORKSPACE_AT`, then an install inside that boundary. I split it into `atCommit` (check workspace at the commit) and `elsewhere` (that plus the install).

How a host check runs:
- **Checkout:** on the workspace's machine, or the check's `machine`, a new agent control `CONTROL_HOST_CHECKOUT` (agent host-check.ts) clones the clone holding the commit into `~/.cawco/host-checks/<run>`, detached at that commit. That source is the workspace itself, or its `atCommit` check workspace on another machine. Git runs with the safe-git flags, and not at all if the source's config holds a key past the allowlist.
- **Install and run:** both go through `CONTROL_RUN_COMMAND` with no workspace ref, so `/bin/sh -c` as the agent's user, outside any boundary. Output, `expect`, `timeoutSec` and queueing work as for every other check. The check's line says `on the host, <machine> at <sha9>`.
- **Pause:** after rebasing onto main, a host check follows main's pause handling. A pause that cancels it runs it again in the same checkout, and an install a pause cut runs again.
- **Cleanup:** every checkout is removed in `runChecks`' `finally` (`CONTROL_HOST_CHECKOUT_REMOVE`). Any left over are removed when the hub's connection ends (beside `abandonCommands`) and when the agent starts.
- **Disk gate:** before writing anything, the agent compares `statfs` against `CAWCO_MIN_FREE_GB` (10 unless set). The refusal reads "<dir> has X GB free, under the N GB a heavy run needs to start (CAWCO_MIN_FREE_GB), so no checkout was made".
- **Hub-only:** all four new controls are in `HUB_WORKSPACE_CONTROLS`.

A leaf already can't change checks; I verified this rather than adding anything:
- delegation-tools.ts `tool()`: `const schema = inputError ? z.strictObject(input, ...) : z.object(input);`. finish_item passes no `inputError`, so it gets a plain `z.object`, which strips unknown keys. Run here: `parse({headline, summary, checks:[{host:true}]})` gives `{"headline":"h","summary":"s"}`.
- Its JSON schema has no `additionalProperties:false`, so a call carrying `checks` is accepted and the field is ignored.
- `finishable` reads `item.checks` from the row.
- `setChecks` refuses anyone but the item's parent.

**2. `inputs: string[]`** on delegate, plus an `inputs` field on handoff. Handoff lists it only to sessions that may delegate; a leaf has no delegate to hand inputs to.
- **Read** on the parent's machine (`CONTROL_INPUTS_READ`, agent inputs.ts) before anything is cut.
- **Written** (`CONTROL_INPUTS_WRITE`) into `$TMPDIR/inputs/` before the session spawns, before a follow-up's brief, and before a handoff goes. A link planted at `inputs` is removed, the folder's real path is checked before each file, and each file is written temp-then-rename.
- **Named** in the brief header ("Your parent's inputs are in $TMPDIR/inputs/: name (from /path)", core `withInputsLine`) and in the start text.
- **Refused** by core `inputDenial`, judged on both the given path and its real path:
  - `credentialStores()`: keys, logins, the hub's secrets;
  - secret file names;
  - on Linux, `LINUX_HOST_PRIVATE`;
  - also: relative paths, folders, two inputs with the same name, more than 50 files, more than 64 MiB.
- **64 MiB cap, my call:** a long session's transcript runs to tens of MB (wire.ts). Base64 of 64 MiB is ~86 MiB per hop, within the 512 MiB wire limit and the 256 MiB bundle cap.
- **Handoff inputs** go through `POST /api/work-items/inputs`, allowed for the item's parent or its project's lead.

## My call: only a session outside every boundary declares a host check
work-items `hostDeclared` returns 403 when the declaring session runs inside a boundary: a work item's workspace, or Caw's lead place (`leadPlaceRef`, passed in as the new `leadPlace` dep). This covers delegate, task attempts and set_item_checks. Without it, a `can_delegate` delegate could escape its boundary through its child's unsandboxed check. Headline: A machine's preview listener now answers only the hub's relay. A request or WebSocket straight to its port gets CawCo's 403. The page, its HMR, port mode and host mode all still work through the hub.

## Mechanism: the existing per-start token, carried as a relay header
**The existing trust.** The agent's hub socket (`.ws("/ws")`, hub server.ts) has no credential of its own, and there is no machine-level secret. The one secret the hub and an agent already share for a listener is the per-start token:
- `const token = crypto.randomUUID();` (server.ts `startListener`).
- It is sent to the agent only inside `callAgent(machineId, PREVIEW_START, [{ instanceId, ...source, token }], …)` on the agent's hub socket.
- The hub keeps it as `upstream: { address, port, token }`. The agent keeps it in its `previews` map, re-reports it in `servingPreviews()` on register, and the hub re-adopts it in `reconcilePreviews`.
- No frame to a browser carries it (`previewFrame` has artifact, address, source and revision only).

It is unguessable, scoped to one listener, dies with it, and already survives agent and hub restarts through the register. So it is the credential, and no second one is invented.

**Hub side** (`packages/hub/src/preview.ts`, `relay`): `headers.set(RELAY_HEADER, at.token)` on every relayed request. The same headers go to `upgradePreview`, so WebSocket upgrades carry it too. Because it uses `set`, a header a browser sends itself is overwritten.

**Agent side** (`packages/agent/src/preview.ts`, `start`):
- The first step of the listener's `fetch` compares the `x-cawco-relay` header with the start token using `timingSafeEqual`. On a miss it answers `CawCo refused this request: a preview opens only through its hub. Open it from the CawCo dashboard or app.` (403) and logs a line through `previewFailed`.
- This runs before the editor-route refusal, before the Host, Origin and Referer rewrite, and for folder previews as well as ports.
- Upgrades go through the same `fetch`, so a direct socket never opens.
- The header is deleted before the request goes upstream, so the app never sees it.
- The listener still binds `0.0.0.0`, so the hub on another machine can reach it.

**Core:** `RELAY_HEADER = "x-cawco-relay"` in `packages/core/src/preview-proxy.ts`, shared by both hops.

**Cutover, one path.** The token is required end to end:
- `startPreview` throws without one.
- `PreviewTarget.upstream.token: string`.
- `ServingPreview.token: string`. `peekPreviews` drops a reported listener without a token, so its target starts a new listener.
- The agent's map and `servingPreviews` hold `token: string`.
- `stopPreview`'s token stays optional, because a stop without one means stop any listener for that session.

## The rule and its sources
A folder counts as rebuilt output when it holds a regular file `CACHEDIR.TAG` whose first 43 bytes are the signature. That signature is set by the Cache Directory Tagging Specification, https://bford.info/cachedir/:
- "The presence of a cache directory tag within a given directory indicates that the *entire* contents of that directory, including any and all subdirectories underneath it, consists of cached information that can be re-generated if necessary from appropriate source material located elsewhere."
- "any tool that has built-in support for cache directory tags is *strongly encouraged* to verify that any file it finds named `CACHEDIR.TAG` is a regular file and actually contains the 43-byte header". The check does both.

Who uses it:
- cargo tags `target/` (https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/pull/8378: "CACHEDIR.TAG is an OS-independent mechanism supported by Borg, restic, GNU Tar").
- pytest writes it into `.pytest_cache` (src/_pytest/cacheprovider.py `CACHEDIR_FILES`), and ruff into its cache.
- restic's `--exclude-caches` "excludes cache directories that are marked with a CACHEDIR.TAG file".

Why not git: there is no git rule that tells a build cache from a person's file. git treats every ignored file as expendable; git-clean(1) says `-X` will "Remove only files ignored by Git… rebuild everything from scratch, but keep manually created files". That is exactly how `.probe/preview/` was lost. git's "precious" class was only ever proposed (the precious-attribute RFC at spinics msg466588, gitgitgadget PR 1627, and the 2025 `clean.exclude` series), and none of it landed.

Where the repository declares it: Kit 3.0's type docs for `outDir` read "The directory that SvelteKit writes files to during `dev` and `build`. You should exclude this directory from version control. @default ".svelte-kit"". adapter-node 6.0.0's `adapt` starts with `fs.rmSync(out, { force: true, recursive: true })`, so the tag is written after `adapt` returns. `apps/dashboard/vite.config.ts` `cacheTagged()` wraps `adapter({ out: BUILD_OUT })` and, after `inner.adapt(builder)`, writes the tag into `builder.config.outDir` and `BUILD_OUT`.
